To put SN 2023iop in the context of other SNe II and H-rich SLSNe, we measure light-curve parameters from the multiband $cgroi$ photometry. The apparent magnitude in each band was first interpolated using Gaussian Processes [243, GP;] with a Matérn-5/2 kernel. The peak epochs and magnitudes were then determined by fitting a weighted second-degree polynomial within a $\pm 75$ day window centered on the GP-derived maximum, with uncertainties obtained from 5000 Monte Carlo draws from the curve-fitting covariance matrix. The peak time depends strongly on wavelength: the light curve peaks first in the $g$ band, at MJD $60155.70\pm 0.86$ , and 22.5 rest-frame days later in the $i$ band (Table 1). Throughout the paper, we use the peak time in the $r$ band as a reference point ( $\rm MJD=60169.63$ ; Table 1). Rest-frame decline timescales, defined as the elapsed time for the flux to fall to a given fraction of its peak value and measured from the GP light curves, are listed in Table 1.

During the decline of the early-time light curve, SN 2023iop’s colors trace the ejecta’s thermal evolution. Up to 150 days after peak brightness, the color reddens steadily. The $g-r$ color increases from $\sim 0.5$ mag near maximum to $\sim 1.5$ –2.0 mag roughly by day +120, tracking the cooling and recombination of the hydrogen envelope. On day +30, SN 2023iop’s $u-g\gtrsim 1.4$ mag and $u-r\gtrsim 2.0$ mag are already far redder than any object in the broad-H $\alpha$ SLSN II sample observed by ZTF at comparable phase [152, $u-g$ spans only $0.3$ – $1.2$ mag and $u-r$ spans $0.3$ – $1.2$ mag;]. SN 2023iop’s day +30 $u-r$ color is instead comparable to the $u-r>2$ mag reached by ordinary SNe II at a similar phase [72, 329, 271]. Once SN 2023iop reaches the plateau, the color settles to $g-r\approx 0.6$ mag and remains constant to within $0.1$ mag between days +250 and +400. The optical-to-near-IR colors ( $r-J$ , $i-J$ , and $z-J$ ) likewise show no significant evolution over the same interval, including across the onset of the rapid decline after day +325, though the large uncertainties and sparse NIR sampling preclude a more nuanced conclusion.

The $r$ -band light curve spans the longest time interval, allowing accurate measurements of the rise and decline timescales. The $e$ -folding rise and decline timescales are $>85.8$ and $77.2\pm 0.7$ rest-frame days, respectively (additional timescales, including band-dependent values, are listed in Table 1). Two properties stand out in the context of H-rich SLSNe. The lower limit on the $r$ -band rest-frame rise time firmly places SN 2023iop among the slowest-rising H-rich SLSNe with broad H $\alpha$ emission lines [139, 152, 228]. However, SN 2023iop’s combination of a very slow rise and a comparatively fast decline breaks the positive rise-decline correlation seen in H-rich SLSNe [228]. This light-curve shape is also markedly different from that of a regular SN II. Instead, SN 2023iop’s light-curve morphology resembles that of SN 1987A, though it is significantly broader and more luminous than even the most extreme 87A-like objects, OGLE-73 and SN 2020faa. In Sections V.5 and V.6, we compare in detail SN 2023iop’s light-curve properties with those of SLSNe-II and 87A-like objects.

### IV.3 Bolometric Light Curve

We constructed the bolometric light curve of SN 2023iop (shown in Panel A of Figure 3) with the estimate_bolometric_luminosity routine in redback [255] version 1.15.1, fitting the extinction-corrected photometry in 5-day observer-frame bins (each with $\geq 3$ measurements) to a single-temperature blackbody parameterized by $\log~T_{\rm BB}$ and $\log~R_{\rm BB}$ , with model magnitudes integrated over the filter transmission curves rather than effective wavelengths. The luminosity of each epoch then follows from the Stefan-Boltzmann law, $L_{\rm bol}=4\pi\sigma R_{\rm BB}^{2}T_{\rm BB}^{4}$ .

This procedure relies on several simplifying assumptions. First, the spectral energy distribution (SED) is a pure blackbody at all wavelengths. Second, $L_{\rm bol}$ includes flux at wavelengths that our data do not cover. Our $griz$ coverage spans only 4700–8960 Å, with the bluest constraint at the $g$ band in 34 of 37 epochs, so both the UV and the IR contributions are pure extrapolation, and the majority of the reported $L_{\rm bol}$ therefore rests on extrapolation rather than on measured flux. As the ejecta cool, the unobserved fraction migrates from the UV to the IR, so the infrared dominates the correction at late times. Although we have detections in the IR, they are too sparse to constrain this extrapolation directly. Third, we apply no line-blanketing correction; because line blanketing suppresses the emergent blue flux relative to a blackbody, the extrapolation likely overestimates the true UV contribution. Finally, the routine discards epochs with a fractional uncertainty on $T_{\rm BB}$ , $R_{\rm BB}$ , or $L_{\rm bol}$ exceeding unity, and six of the 37 surviving epochs rely on fewer than three filters, including one based on a single band, so their temperatures are weakly constrained.

At peak brightness, SN 2023iop reached a luminosity of $(4.0\pm 1.0)\times 10^{43}\,\rm erg\,s^{-1}$ , and integrating over the entire light curve yields a radiated energy of $(4.3\pm 0.3)\times 10^{50}~\rm erg$ . The radiated energy is a strict lower limit. If SN 2023iop’s luminosity was (2– $3)\times 10^{43}\,\rm erg\,s^{-1}$ between the first detection (day $-87.6$ ) and the first epoch of the bolometric light curve (day $-48$ ), the radiated energy increases by $\sim 20\%$ . The uncertain explosion date may further increase the radiated energy, probably bringing it closer to $\rm 10^{51}~erg$ . While SN 2023iop has a low peak absolute magnitude for an H-rich SLSN [139, 152, 228], the lower limit on its radiated energy places it in the upper half of the observed distribution of H-rich SLSNe with broad Balmer emission lines [152].

*Figure 3: Bolometric light curve (panel A), and evolution of the blackbody photosphere’s radius (panel B) and temperature (panel C). The gray-shaded region indicates the time interval where the blackbody radius and temperature could be measured.*

Such an energy release is difficult to reconcile with a neutrino-driven explosion. The energy budget of a neutrino-driven explosion is set by the gravitational binding energy released when the neutron star forms, $\sim 3\times 10^{53}~\rm erg$ . Because the neutron-star mass distribution is narrow, this budget is fixed to within a factor of $\sim 2$ [166, 220, 141]. Only a small fraction of it reaches the ejecta. Current simulations of neutrino-driven explosions convert $\sim 1\%$ of this budget into ejecta kinetic energy, or $\lesssim 2\times 10^{51}~\rm erg$ [33, 40, 141]. A similarly small fraction of that kinetic energy is radiated. Ordinary SNe II emit only $\sim 10^{49}~\rm erg$ [223, 184], about $1\%$ of their kinetic energy [156, 185].

Reproducing the $\gtrsim 4\times 10^{50}~\rm erg$ radiated by SN 2023iop would therefore require the combined neutrino-to-ejecta coupling and kinetic-to-radiation conversion efficiency to be $\sim 50$ times larger than in normal SNe II. Such an increase could not occur silently. A substantially larger explosion energy would manifest itself in higher ejecta velocities, and a more efficient conversion of kinetic energy into radiation would typically require strong ejecta-CSM interaction, which would generally imprint clear signatures on the spectra. Neither is observed: the photospheric velocities of SN 2023iop are typical of normal SNe II (Section IV.4.3), and its spectra show no evidence of strong interaction (Section IV.4.2). A purely neutrino-driven origin therefore appears highly contrived. Instead, the energetics point to an additional energy source: weak or geometrically confined ejecta-CSM interaction, a contribution from a compact object (a rapidly spinning neutron star or an accreting black hole), or a rare explosion channel (e.g., a PISN). We discuss these scenarios in Section V.4.

Ongoing interaction between the ejecta and dusty CSM would be expected to produce a mid-infrared (MIR) excess from thermal dust emission. SN 2023iop is not detected in the MIR (Appendix, Table 6). WISE $W1$ and $W2$ imaging obtained at day $\sim 295$ yields $3\sigma$ upper limits of 41 and $128~\mu$ Jy, respectively. Neither band shows an excess over the optical and NIR SED, arguing against strong ongoing CSM interaction at this epoch. The limits are shallow, however, and exclude only a luminous warm-dust component.

Panels 3.B and 3.C in Figure 3 show the evolution of the blackbody radius and temperature computed with Redback. The temperature evolution is well described by a linear decline of $1800\pm 100~\rm K\,(100~day)^{-1}$ , whereas the extent of the photosphere follows a piecewise linear function: (i) a linear expansion of $4300\pm 200~\rm km\,s^{-1}$ up to $57\pm 3$ days after peak, reaching almost $9\times 10^{15}~\rm cm$ , and (ii) a linear decline of $6500\pm 1200~\rm km\,s^{-1}$ later. The expansion velocity is similar to that extracted from the absorption minima of Fe II $\lambda$ 5018 (Section IV.4.3). Although SN 2023iop’s light curve is similar to that of 87A-like objects, the maximum blackbody radius of $9\times 10^{15}~\rm cm$ is 15 times larger than that of SN 2018hna (regular 87A-like; D. Xiang et al. 323) and 2–4 times larger than that of the extreme 87A-like SNe OGLE-73 and SN 2020faa [324, 251]. We will discuss the light-curve properties in more detail in Section V.6.

### IV.4 Spectroscopy

#### IV.4.1 Spectral Template Matching

Template matching of the NOT/ALFOSC spectrum obtained on day $+13.6$ with SN II templates using NGSF [117] and SNID-SAGE [285] yields excellent matches to normal SNe IIP, most notably SN 1999em, but also to the prototypical 87A-like event SN 1987A (Figure 4). Repeating this analysis for all subsequent spectra yields similarly good matches with SNe II throughout the entire spectroscopic sequence [250, 221, 6, e.g., SNe 2004et, 2005cs, 2015bs, 2016hmq, 2018emt, 2018kpo;], including the final spectrum obtained on day $+326$ (Figure 4). Good matches with SN 1987A are also recovered at most epochs (maximum light epoch shown in Figure 4), although no satisfactory SN 1987A match is found for the day $+326$ spectrum. This close correspondence demonstrates that, despite its extreme luminosity and unusually broad light curve, SN 2023iop occupies a familiar spectroscopic regime and closely resembles common SNe II during the photospheric phase.

For spectra obtained up to $\sim 100$ days after maximum brightness, the phases of best-matching normal SNe II are typically $\sim 16$ days after peak (range: 9–50 days), with no correlation between the template phase and the actual phase of SN 2023iop. At later epochs, the preferred matches are with SN II spectra obtained at $\sim+74$ days. This behavior is noteworthy given that normal SNe II generally reach maximum light within a few days of explosion and evolve substantially faster thereafter [249, 121, 184, 130, 90]. Therefore, the discrepancy directly reflects SN 2023iop’s extraordinarily slow spectroscopic evolution. A similar trend is found when restricting the comparison to SN 1987A. In that case, the preferred matches correspond to spectra of SN 1987A acquired $\sim 80$ days before maximum light, indicating the smaller extent of the hydrogen envelope in normal 87A-like SNe.

#### IV.4.2 Spectroscopic Sequence

Figure 5 presents the optical spectral sequence for SN 2023iop, spanning $-51.4$ to $+380$ rest-frame days relative to peak light.33 3 We omit displaying the epochs on days +461.2 and +483.8 because they did not exhibit any SN features; they are discussed in Section IV.1. Already at the earliest epoch (day $-51.4$ ), the spectrum exhibits well-developed P-Cygni profiles in the Balmer lines, while metal lines are present but comparatively weak. Over this extended interval, the spectra show a clear blue-to-red evolution driven by cooling, accompanied by a rich set of features that evolve very slowly and closely track SN 2023iop’s gradual photometric evolution. Line profiles and relative strengths change only moderately over tens of days, indicating persistent photospheric conditions well beyond epochs at which most core-collapse SNe enter the nebular phase.

To facilitate line identification, we focus on the X-shooter spectrum from day $+71.7$ in Figure 6 and use A. Singh et al. [270] as a point of reference. At this phase, Balmer features remain prominent, while metal absorption lines from Fe II, Ti II, Sc II, and Ba II are relatively weak. Spectra obtained with Keck/LRIS, MagE, and X-shooter provide high sensitivity in the $u$ band. Essentially, they show no detectable flux blueward of 3500 Å (rest frame), besides a minor contribution from the host galaxy. In addition, the Keck/DEIMOS, LRIS, MagE, and X-shooter data have high S/N and high spectral resolutions ranging from $R=1000$ to 8000. They reveal no evidence of narrow Balmer emission lines44 4 The two NOT/ALFOSC spectra (days $+13.6$ and $+37.2$ ) exhibit two sharp features around the peak of the H $\alpha$ P-Cygni profile. At SN 2023iop’s redshift, the rest-frame H $\alpha$ line is observed at $\sim 7234$ Å, coinciding with the $\sim 7200$ Å H2O telluric absorption complex. Under typical observing conditions at Observatorio del Roque de los Muchachos, this can result in measurable telluric absorption that could be misidentified as narrow, low-velocity absorption components. Observations of a telluric standard would have been needed to correct for this. The FORS2 observation on day +326 was done in very good conditions (precipitable water vapor $\approx 2$ mm). That water vapor indeed affects this wavelength region is best seen in the high-resolution MagE and X-shooter spectra. commonly associated with SNe IIn. Both an excess flux below 3500 Å or the presence of narrow Balmer emission would be indicative of ongoing CSM interaction [103, 276], but neither signature is observed. Together with the close resemblance to standard SNe II (Section IV.4.1), these observations show no direct spectroscopic evidence for ongoing CSM interaction during the observed epochs. This disfavors CSM interaction as a driver of SN 2023iop’s high luminosity or unusually broad light curve, albeit the absorption-to-emission ratio of H $\alpha$ is unusually small (Section IV.4.3).

We obtained two epochs of NIR spectroscopy on days $+71.7$ and $+99.9$ . No significant spectral evolution is observed between these epochs, and only a few weak features are detected. For this reason, we show only the day $+71.7$ spectrum in Figure 6. The dominant transitions are Pa $\alpha$ and Pa $\gamma$ , while Pa $\beta$ falls in a region strongly affected by atmospheric absorption.

On day +99.9, the forbidden [Ca II] $\lambda\lambda 7291$ , 7324 doublet becomes visible and subsequently strengthens. By day +135.3, [O I] $\lambda\lambda 6300$ , 6364 is also clearly detected. It may have been present at earlier phases, but blending with neighboring features (e.g., the P-Cygni profile of H $\alpha$ ) likely hinders its identification.

Intriguingly, the late-time spectra show the coexistence of nebular and photospheric signatures. Although forbidden emission from [O I] and [Ca II] is clearly established by day +135, strong H $\alpha$ emission, H $\alpha$ absorption, and Fe II $\lambda$ 5018 remain visible even in the spectrum at day +326. This combination indicates that a substantial fraction of the ejecta remains optically thick while nebular emission becomes increasingly prominent, demonstrating that SN 2023iop evolves much more slowly toward the nebular phase than typical SNe II.

#### IV.4.3 Line Evolution

Next, we zoom in on the evolution of the Fe II and H $\alpha$ lines, which trace the bulk ejecta (Fe II) and the fastest-moving H-rich material (H $\alpha$ ), respectively. Among the three strong Fe II transitions between 4900 and 5200 Å (rest frame), Fe II $\lambda$ 5018 is the least blended and most straightforward to measure. To quantify the evolution of these lines, we normalize the spectra around each feature, apply a mild Savitzky-Golay smoothing filter, and measure the velocity-space location of the absorption minimum, the full width at half-maximum intensity (FWHM), and the EW (all in the rest frame). For H $\alpha$ , we additionally measure the FWHM and EW of the emission component.

Figure 7 places these measurements in the context of the light-curve evolution of SN 2023iop (panel 7.A), together with the evolution of the blackbody radius and temperature (panels 7.B and 7.C). The corresponding measurements are listed in Table 12 of the Appendix. As discussed in Section IV.3, the photosphere of SN 2023iop cooled from $\sim 7000$ K on day $-48$ to $\sim 4500$ K by day $+100$ , while its radius expanded to $\sim 9\times 10^{15}$ cm around day $+57$ before receding into deeper layers of the ejecta, consistent with the behavior expected of a recombination-powered photosphere [10].

Panel 7.D shows the evolution of the absorption-minimum velocities for Fe II and H $\alpha$ . The velocity of Fe II $\lambda$ 5018 declines smoothly from $5600\,~\rm km\,s^{-1}$ on day $+13.6$ to $3100\,~\rm km\,s^{-1}$ on day $+139.8$ , consistent with the photosphere receding into deeper ejecta layers. This evolution is broadly consistent with the expansion velocity inferred from the blackbody-radius evolution ( $4300\pm 200~\rm km\,s^{-1}$ measured from the data before the blackbody radius peaked) during the phase in which the blackbody radius increases approximately linearly. Beyond day $+139.8$ , the measured Fe II velocity remains approximately constant at $\sim 3300~\rm km\,s^{-1}$ . The slight increase at late times may be an artifact of the lower S/N of the MMT/Binospec spectra. In contrast, the H $\alpha$ absorption velocity remains remarkably constant at 7600– $8200\,~\rm km\,s^{-1}$ between days $+13.6$ and $+139.8$ , showing no measurable deceleration.

Such a velocity offset is common in SNe II and reflects H $\alpha$ forming at larger radii in the extended H envelope than metal lines such as Fe II, which form closer to the photosphere and track its recession more closely [78, 121]. In those objects, however, both velocities decline with time. At later epochs, the H $\alpha$ absorption velocity can no longer be measured reliably because of the increasing contribution from [O I] $\lambda\lambda 6300$ , 6364 emission (Figure 5).

Although the velocities of H $\alpha$ and Fe II evolve differently, both line widths decrease with time (panel 7.E). The same behavior is observed for the emission component of the H $\alpha$ P-Cygni profile. Because H $\alpha$ remains strongly in emission, its width can be tracked throughout the entire spectroscopic campaign. The width of the H $\alpha$ emission component closely follows the photometric evolution: it decreases between maximum light and approximately day $+100$ ; remains nearly constant until day $+326$ ; and then drops abruptly from $6600\pm 100$ to $4300\pm 300~\rm km\,s^{-1}$ (Appendix, Table 12). This transition coincides with a rapid fading of the light curve (Section IV.2). The dramatic narrowing of the H $\alpha$ emission profile occurs only during this late-time decline. By contrast, during the similarly rapid decline observed between days $+50$ and $+100$ , the FWHM decreases by only $500\pm 300~\rm km\,s^{-1}$ (Appendix, Table 12).

Panel 7.F presents the EW evolution. The EW of the H $\alpha$ emission component increases monotonically from $268$ to $902$ Å between days $+13.6$ and $+135.3$ , whereas the EW of the absorption component decreases from $54$ to $22$ Å. Consequently, the absorption-to-emission EW ratio ( $a/e$ ), a commonly used diagnostic of the Type II SN Balmer-line diversity [121, 67], drops from $0.20$ to $0.02$ – $0.03$ over the same period. Thus, the H $\alpha$ profile is already emission-dominated at the earliest epoch and becomes progressively more so over time. In contrast, Fe II $\lambda$ 5018 remains weak throughout the plateau phase, with EWs of only $7$ – $10$ Å, declining further to $1$ – $2$ Å by day $+140$ . Two later measurements (days $+296$ and $+326$ ) suggest a restrengthening of Fe II. However, comparing the profiles of Fe II $\lambda$ 4924 and Fe II $\lambda$ 5018 indicates that an additional line may contribute to the apparent strengthening of Fe II $\lambda$ 5018. At even later epochs, the H $\alpha$ EW declines rapidly. Although an increasing contribution from the host-galaxy continuum may exaggerate this trend as the SN fades, and the exact EW measured in the day +380 spectrum is sensitive to the details of the late-time data reduction, the simultaneous sharp decrease in the H $\alpha$ line width is largely insensitive to these effects. The concurrent declines in both EW and FWHM therefore suggest that the weakening of the line is at least partly intrinsic.

Taken together, the constant H $\alpha$ absorption velocity (Panel 7.D), the growing emission dominance of the profile (Panel 7.F), and the widening velocity offset from Fe II (Panel 7.D) are difficult to reconcile with line formation in a single, homologously expanding photosphere. Previously studied 87A-like events show no comparable evolution [270]. The observations instead suggest that an increasing fraction of the H $\alpha$ emission arises in a region external to the recombining ejecta traced by Fe II, such as CSM or a cool dense shell [59, 103, 276, 211]. Discriminating among these configurations requires tailored radiative-transfer modeling.

#### IV.4.4 Line Profiles

The spectrum on day +326 provides the highest-S/N view of the emission-line profiles at late times and offers a direct probe of the kinematic structure of the inner ejecta (Figure 8). Nebular emission-line profiles are known to be sensitive to the geometry and velocity structure of the emitting material [176, 302, 97, 303], and different ionic species can trace distinct regions of the ejecta [198, 143].

The forbidden lines share a common kinematic signature. [O I] $\lambda$ 5577, [O I] $\lambda\lambda$ 6300, 6364 and O I $\lambda$ 7774 are all single-peaked, with comparable widths. [O I] $\lambda$ 5577 is blueshifted by $\sim 1000~\rm km\,s^{-1}$ relative to the systemic velocity, as is the blue maximum of the emission complex at 7300 Å. H $\alpha$ is also single-peaked, but remains optically thick at this phase, so its profile is shaped by radiative transfer rather than by the distribution of the emitting material. It shows a mild displacement toward redder velocities.

The spectral resolution does not permit a detailed decomposition of the individual components. The recurrence of similar offsets and widths nonetheless indicates that the line-forming regions are not symmetric about the systemic velocity, and that several transitions originate in related kinematic structures.

The 7300 Å complex is the exception. Besides the blue maximum described above, it shows a second maximum near $+2600~\rm km\,s^{-1}$ , separated from the first by $\sim 3000~\rm km\,s^{-1}$ . This component was absent up to day +139.8 and fully developed by day +296.2, when our coverage resumed after solar conjunction. No other feature in the spectrum shows a comparable second maximum. We tentatively attribute it to [Ni II] $\lambda$ 7378 from stable 58Ni rather than to [Ca II] $\lambda$ 7324 (Section V.3).

### IV.5 Spectropolarimetry

*Figure 9: Spectropolarimetry of SN 2023iop on day +37.3, obtained with FORS2 (50 Å binning). The spectrum shows a high level of continuum polarization, 0.8–1%, measured in line-free regions around H $\alpha$ . The gray vertical stripes and the “ $\earth$ ” symbol mark the telluric A and B bands.*

Spectropolarimetry probes the geometry of the photosphere and line-forming regions. Figure 9 displays the spectropolarimetric observation obtained on day +37.3.

Despite the modest S/N of the polarization spectrum, SN 2023iop exhibits significant continuum polarization. This interpretation is supported by the noticeable depolarization over the H $\alpha$ emission line. To first order, SN line emission is expected to be unpolarized, so it dilutes any underlying continuum polarization, causing the observed dip. We estimate the continuum polarization ( $P$ ) from line‑poor wavelength intervals on either side of the H $\alpha$ P‑Cygni profile using a uniform 50 Å spectral binning. In the 5800–6200 Å (rest frame) interval we measure $P=0.83\pm 0.09~\%$ , while in the 7400–7800 Å region we find $P=0.76\pm 0.14~\%$ . The inverse‑variance‑weighted mean of these wavelength intervals is $P=0.81\pm 0.08~\%$ . A measurement from a less-rebinned (25 Å) spectrum yields a consistent but slightly higher value ( $P=0.96\pm 0.08~\%$ ), indicating that the inferred continuum polarization is not an artifact of the chosen binning scheme.

The observed global level of polarization is unlikely to be dominated by interstellar polarization (ISP), which produces a smooth, broad-band effect. Instead, the depolarization across the H $\alpha$ emission line can be used to constrain the ISP contribution. At the line peak, the spectrum is consistent with $Q\approx U\approx 0$ , indicating a low combined ISP along the line of sight. This is supported by the low Galactic extinction $E(B-V)=0.044$ mag, corresponding to an expected Milky Way ISP of $9\times E(B-V)\leq 0.4\%$ [266]. In addition, the C. Heiles [127] catalog contains one star within $4^{\circ}$ of the SN position. It has a low polarization of only $P=0.070\pm 0.035\%$ , consistent with interstellar polarization. Together, these checks leave no evidence for a significant ISP contribution from either the Milky Way or SN 2023iop’s host galaxy. Finally, the presence of line-locked depolarization across H $\alpha$ demonstrates that the continuum polarization is intrinsic to the SN and not caused by the lunar sky background, which would not reproduce such spectral features.

In addition to the depolarization observed across the H $\alpha$ emission component, the polarization spectrum shows an increase in polarization coincident with the absorption minimum of the P‑Cygni profile. This behavior indicates that the H‑rich ejecta are themselves aspherical. In this scenario, absorption by material along the line of sight preferentially removes unpolarized continuum photons, thereby enhancing the fractional contribution of scattered, and hence polarized, light originating from the asymmetric limb of the ejecta [191, e.g.,]. The resulting polarization peak at the absorption trough provides independent evidence that the line‑forming region shares the global asymmetry of the continuum-forming photosphere.

The measured continuum polarization of $P\approx 0.8$ –1.0 % implies a substantial departure from spherical symmetry in the ejecta [132, 142]. Canonical SNe II are typically consistent with negligible continuum polarization during the photospheric phase, with polarization rising only once the photosphere recedes below the hydrogen envelope at the transition to the nebular phase [61, 205, e.g.,]. This timing depends on the thickness of the hydrogen envelope. For a more massive envelope, such as inferred for SN 2023iop under the PISN interpretation (Section V.4.1), this transition would be expected even later. SN 2023iop’s significant continuum polarization already on day +37.3 is therefore not straightforwardly explained by a receding photosphere alone. A bipolar explosion offers a more direct precedent: the Type IIP SNe 2012aw and 2021yja show comparably high polarization already during the plateau phase, attributed to an energetic polar ejecta component that dominates before the bulk equatorial ejecta emerges at later times [206].

In contrast, 87A-like events are known to display significant polarization at comparable epochs. SN 1987A exhibited continuum polarization of $\sim 0.6$ % in the $R$ and $I$ bands between maximum light and several tens of days thereafter [142], a behavior attributed to large‑scale asymmetry in the ejecta [132, 312]. Similarly, the 87A‑like SN 2018hna showed significant optical polarization during the photospheric phase [190]. The somewhat higher continuum polarization measured for SN 2023iop suggests an even more pronounced deviation from spherical symmetry. This could reflect a larger global axial ratio, or bipolar or lopsided structures imprinted on the hydrogen envelope by asymmetric energy deposition or shock propagation during the explosion [132, 313], similar to the bipolar geometry recently inferred for the Type IIP SNe 2012aw and 2021yja [206]. However, alternative interpretations involving asymmetric excitation or radiative-transfer effects without a strongly jet-driven explosion cannot be excluded [62, 79]. A comparably high continuum polarization ( $\sim 0.8$ %) has, for instance, been attributed not to intrinsic ejecta asymmetry but to an aspherical circumstellar disk in the luminous, long-lived Type II SN 2021irp [245].

*Figure 10: SN 2023iop in the Stokes $Q-U$ plane on day +37.3 (binning 50 Å). The points are color-coded by wavelength. Concentric circles show polarization degrees ranging from 0.5 to 2.5%. The photosphere shows a clear departure from spherical symmetry, but the absence of a dominant axis does not indicate an axially symmetric geometry.*

While the continuum polarization amplitude clearly indicates significant asphericity in the photosphere, further constraints on the underlying geometry can be obtained from the distribution of points in the $Q-U$ plane (Figure 10). Although the data are somewhat noisy, the measurements do not reveal a clear dominant axis indicative of simple axial symmetry, suggesting that the ejecta geometry may be more complex than a single coherent axisymmetric structure.

### IV.6 Multiwavelength Limits

To probe nonthermal emission, circumstellar interaction [55, 59, 60], and possible central engine activity [83, 179, 216], as outlined in Section V.7, we examined the X-ray and radio upper limits derived for SN 2023iop.

We find an unabsorbed X-ray flux limit of $<1.2\times 10^{-13}~{\rm erg\,cm^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$ on day +30.3 (0.3–10 keV; Appendix, Section A.5), corresponding to a luminosity of $<4\times 10^{42}~{\rm erg\,s^{-1}}$ at $z=0.1020$ . This limit is comparable to X-ray nondetections of H-poor SLSNe [169, 181], but lies more than two orders of magnitude above the X-ray luminosities seen in luminous SNe IIn [48]. D. Alp et al. [4] reported that SN ejecta can remain optically thick to bound-free absorption across the whole 0.3–10 keV band for years to decades, so these data cannot test a central engine regardless of depth. An external shock is not screened by the ejecta, but at day +30.3 the ejecta had reached only a few $\times 10^{15}$ cm, well inside the CSM inferred from the late-time light curve, so no interaction signal was expected either.

Centimeter-wave follow-up observations with the AMI-LA on days +84.4 and +102.6 yielded a nondetection with a root mean square (RMS) of 48 $\mu$ Jy (Appendix, Section A.4). They translate to a $3\sigma$ spectral luminosity limit of $L_{\nu}<4.4\times 10^{28}~{\rm erg\,s^{-1}\,Hz^{-1}}$ at 15.5 GHz. The most radio-luminous SNe, such as the Type Ic-BL SN PTF11qcj [65, $\sim 10^{29}~{\rm erg\,s^{-1}\,Hz^{-1}}$ ;], reach luminosities above this limit, while the H-poor SLSN PTF10hgi [88, $\sim 10^{28}~{\rm erg\,s^{-1}\,Hz^{-1}}$ ;] sits below it. As in the X-rays, absorption rather than depth sets the constraint, though for different reasons in the two channels. For a central engine, the ejecta are optically thick to free-free absorption at centimeter wavelengths [197, 203, 216, 179], and, given the probable large ejecta masses of extreme 87A-like events (Section V.1.1), they remain so for one to two decades (Section V.7). An external shock is not screened by the ejecta, but CSM dense enough to power the light curve is itself optically thick to free-free absorption at 15.5 GHz at this epoch. Radio emission from strongly interacting SNe accordingly is expected to peak only after years [60]. Neither channel is therefore constrained at the levels of interest here.

## V Discussion

### V.1 Ejecta and Nickel Mass: Constraints from Photometric Timescales

#### V.1.1 Ejecta Mass

Before turning to detailed power-source models, we derive a basic estimate of SN 2023iop’s total ejecta mass from its light-curve rise time. SN 2023iop’s unusually slow rise may imply a long photon diffusion time through the homologously expanding ejecta. In the diffusion formalism of W. D. Arnett [13], this timescale is given by

$$ t_{\rm d}\approx\left(\frac{2\kappa M_{\rm ej}}{\beta cv}\right)^{1/2}, $$

where $\kappa$ is the effective opacity, $M_{\rm ej}$ is the ejecta mass, $v$ is a characteristic ejecta velocity, and $c$ is the speed of light. The dimensionless constant $\beta\approx 13.8$ depends on the ejecta density structure [13]. If radiative diffusion primarily governs the rise, $t_{\rm rise}\approx t_{\rm d}$ , the ejecta mass is given by

$$ M_{\rm ej}\approx\frac{\beta cvt_{\rm rise}^{2}}{2\kappa}. $$

The ejecta mass then scales as

$$ \displaystyle M_{\rm ej} \displaystyle\approx 12.8~M_{\odot} \displaystyle\times\left(\frac{t_{\rm rise}}{90~{\rm day}}\right)^{2}\left(\frac{v}{6000~\rm km\,s^{-1}}\right)\left(\frac{\kappa}{0.3~{\rm cm^{2}~g^{-1}}}\right)^{-1}. $$

Adopting the lower limit on the rise time of $\sim 88$ days (Section IV.2; Table 1) and assuming $v=6000~\rm km\,s^{-1}$ (Section IV.4.3; Appendix Table 12), and an effective gray opacity $\kappa=0.3~\rm cm^{2}\,g^{-1}$ (consistent with values used in semianalytic models for both regular SNe II and 87A-like SNe, e.g., A. P. Nagy & J. Vinkó 207), yields an ejecta mass of $>12\,M_{\odot}$ .

#### V.1.2 Nickel Mass

In SNe powered by the decay chain ${}^{56}{\rm Ni}\rightarrow{{}^{56}{\rm Co}}\rightarrow{{}^{56}{\rm Fe}}$ , the peak luminosity is determined by the amount of radioactive nickel. SN 2023iop resembles SNe 1987A and 2018hna in light-curve shape but exceeds their peak luminosity by $\sim 3.7$ –4.0 mag (Table 4). If this offset were entirely due to radioactive decay, and adopting as calibrators the nickel yields of SNe 1987A and 2018hna66 6 A. Singh et al. [270] reported a nickel yield of $0.087~M_{\odot}$ , assuming a distance modulus of 30.52. In this paper, we assume a distance modulus of 30.11 (Table 4), which reduces SN 2018hna’s nickel yield by $\sim 31\%$ . ( $0.07$ and $0.06\,M_{\odot}$ , respectively; P. Bouchet et al. 34, N. B. Suntzeff et al. 289, A. Singh et al. 270), the implied 56Ni mass for SN 2023iop is

$$ M_{\rm Ni}({\rm SN\,2023iop})\approx M_{\rm Ni,ref}\times 10^{0.4\,\Delta m}, $$

where $\Delta m$ is the peak-magnitude offset relative to each calibrator. This gives $M_{\rm Ni}({\rm SN\,2023iop})\approx 2.2\,M_{\odot}$ for both calibrators.

The initial post-maximum decline resembles the end of the recombination phase in SNe II (Section V.6.1). Afterward, SN 2023iop faded by only $0.2$ mag (100 day)-1 between days +150 and +325, markedly slower than the $\sim 1$ mag (100 day)-1 expected for pure 56Co decay, before dropping sharply thereafter (Section IV.2). Radioactive decay alone therefore did not power SN 2023iop throughout this interval. The last detection of SN 2023iop, on day +377.1, nonetheless provides an independent, and potentially tighter, upper bound on the nucleosynthesized nickel mass. By this epoch all 56Ni has decayed into 56Co, whose $e$ -folding time is $\tau_{\rm Co}=111.3$ days [204], so the decay luminosity reduces to

$$ L_{\rm decay}(t)\approx M_{\rm Ni}\times 1.33\times 10^{43}~{\rm erg\,s^{-1}}\,M_{\odot}^{-1}\times e^{-t/\tau_{\rm Co}}, $$

where $t$ is measured from the explosion rather than from maximum light.

SN 2023iop’s rise of $>88$ days (Section IV.2) places the last detection at $>465$ days after explosion, and attributing the entire observed luminosity to radioactive decay then gives $M_{\rm Ni}\lesssim 2\,M_{\odot}$ , comparable to the peak-based bound. This remains conservative for two reasons. The explosion may have preceded the first detection by considerably longer, and the luminosity adopted here does not capture the full bolometric output, since the infrared contribution is unconstrained by our data at these epochs (Section IV.3).

Equation 5 further assumes complete $\gamma$ -ray trapping. A. Jerkstrand et al. [147] reported that SNe II become optically thin to $\gamma$ -rays $\sim 1$ yr after explosion, and PISNe only after $\sim 2$ yr, owing to their more massive ejecta. At $>1.2$ years after explosion, SN 2023iop lies within this transition even for a very massive progenitor, so trapping is unlikely to be complete. This would raise the nickel mass derived from the tail, relaxing the bound further.

The upper end of these nickel-mass estimates is inconsistent with a neutrino-driven explosion and instead requires the PISN channel [101, 17, 242], which we discuss in Section V.4.1. A nickel yield of a few tenths of a solar mass, or lower, cannot be excluded. Radioactive decay would then not be the primary power source at any phase, and another energy source would be required.

### V.2 Oxygen Mass: Constraints from Late-time Spectroscopy

Estimating the core oxygen mass from the nebular [O I] $\lambda\lambda 6300,6364$ doublet is a commonly used method for constraining the progenitor mass [300, 171, 146]. The observed doublet ratio contains key information regarding the optical depth of the line-forming gas. In the optically thin limit, the flux ratio is $F_{6300}/F_{6364}=3$ , whereas optically thick emission drives this value toward unity.

From our spectrum at day +326, we measure $F_{6300}/F_{6364}\approx 2.3$ . This suggests that the observed doublet ratio lies near the boundary between the optically thin and thick regimes. However, residual H $\alpha$ absorption and dust formation may partially suppress the 6364 Å component, making the intrinsic ratio uncertain. We therefore evaluate the oxygen mass under both regimes separately.

#### Optically thin regime

In the optically thin limit, the neutral oxygen (O I) mass can be derived from the combined luminosity of the [O I] $\lambda\lambda 6300,6364$ doublet using the analytical approximation of A. Uomoto & R. P. Kirshner [300],

$$ M_{\rm O\,I}\simeq 10^{-4}\left(\frac{L_{6300+6364}}{10^{38}~{\rm erg~s^{-1}}}\right)\exp\!\left(\frac{2.28\times 10^{4}~{\rm K}}{T}\right)M_{\odot}, $$

which reproduces detailed NLTE (non-local thermal equilibrium) spectral calculations to within $\sim 30\%$ under optically thin conditions [146, 144, 262].

To constrain the oxygen temperature $T$ , one can use the flux ratio between the [O I] $\lambda 5577$ and [O I] $\lambda\lambda 6300,6364$ transitions. Assuming both of these transitions to be in LTE with respect to the ground-state, one obtains Equation 2 of A. Jerkstrand et al. [146],

$$ \frac{L_{5577}}{L_{6300,6364}}\approx 38\,\frac{\beta_{5577}}{\beta_{6300,6364}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{25790~{\rm K}}{T}\right), $$

where $\beta$ denotes the Sobolev escape probability [ $\beta=(1-\exp(-\tau_{\lambda}))/\tau_{\lambda}$ and $\tau_{\lambda}$ being the Sobolev optical depth]. The lower level of [O I] $\lambda\lambda 6300,6364$ is in the ground state, whereas the lower level of [O I] $\lambda 5577$ is an excited state. This difference implies $\beta_{5577}>\beta_{6300,6364}$ [143]. Since we are evaluating in the optically thin limit, we assume $\beta_{6300,6364}\approx 1$ , so it follows that also $\beta_{5577}\approx 1$ . Our line luminosity measurements (Table 2) then yield a gas temperature of $T\approx 4250$ K.

Crucially, we deem it unlikely that [O I] $\lambda 5577$ can be approximated as being in LTE for our +326 d spectrum. As discussed by A. Jerkstrand et al. [146], this transition has a large critical electron density (above which the lines form in LTE), $n_{e,\rm crit}=\beta_{5577}\times$ 108 cm-3, with [O I] $\lambda\lambda 6300,6364$ having $n_{e,\rm crit}=\beta_{6300,6364}\times$ 3 $\times$ 106 cm-3. This can be compared to, for example, PISN models by A. Jerkstrand et al. [147], where O-rich zones have $n_{e}\approx 10^{6}$ – 107 cm-3 at 400 days post explosion, or to the CCSN models of S. Barmentloo & A. Jerkstrand [18], which have a similar range of $n_{e}$ . If [O I] $\lambda 5577$ is out of LTE, this leads to an underestimate of the oxygen temperature, so that $T\approx 4250$ K should be understood as a strict lower limit, and thus in turn any estimate of the oxygen mass for the optically thin limit as an upper limit. Keeping this in mind, Equation 6 yields for $T\gtrsim 4250$ K a mass of $M^{\rm thin}_{\rm O\,I}\lesssim 2.8~M_{\odot}$ . Here we do assume that [O I] $\lambda\lambda 6300,6364$ is in LTE, which from the discussion above is plausible, but also not guaranteed.

#### Optically thick regime

If the [O I] doublet is optically thick, the emergent line luminosity no longer scales linearly with oxygen mass. Instead, a strict lower limit is obtained by setting the Sobolev optical depth [277] of the doublet to at least unity,

$$ \tau_{\rm S}=\frac{1}{8\pi}\frac{g_{k}}{g_{l}}A_{\lambda}\lambda^{3}n_{l}t\gtrsim 1, $$

where $g_{k}$ and $g_{l}$ are the statistical weights of the upper and lower levels, $A_{\lambda}$ is the Einstein spontaneous emission coefficient, $n_{l}$ is the lower-state population density, and $t$ is the elapsed time since explosion. This expression is valid as long as $n_{u}\ll n_{l}$ , which holds provided $E_{u}-E_{l}\gg kT$ . Assuming the lower state is in LTE, which is well justified given that it lies within the ground-state term, the population density is

$$ n_{l}=\frac{M_{\rm ion}}{\mu m_{p}}\frac{1}{V_{\rm emit}}\frac{g_{l}}{Z(T)}\exp(-E_{l}/kT), $$

where $\mu$ is the atomic weight of oxygen, $Z(T)$ is the partition function, $E_{l}$ is the energy of the lower level above the ground state, and $V_{\rm emit}\equiv{4\pi}/{3}\,(v_{\rm O}t)^{3}f_{\rm O}$ is the emitting volume under the assumption of homologous expansion, with $f_{\rm O}$ the oxygen filling factor and $v_{\rm O}$ the characteristic velocity derived from the [O I] profile. Because both lower levels lie within the ground-state term ( $E_{l}/k\lesssim 230$ K), the Boltzmann factor is close to unity at the temperatures of interest, and we set it to unity in what follows.

The two doublet components share the same upper level but differ in their transition probabilities, with $A_{6300}\approx 3\,A_{6364}$ , so that $\tau_{6364}<\tau_{6300}$ at any given oxygen mass. A genuinely optically thick doublet requires both components to satisfy $\tau_{\rm S}\gtrsim 1$ ; therefore, we impose this condition on the weaker $\lambda 6364$ . Evaluating Equations 8 and 9 for $\lambda 6300$ alone would give $M_{\rm O}>151\,f_{\rm O}\,M_{\odot}$ , whereas imposing the condition on $\lambda 6364$ yields

$$ M_{\rm O}^{\rm thick}>455\left(\frac{v_{\rm O}}{4000\,~\rm km\,s^{-1}}\right)^{3}\left(\frac{t}{420\,\rm day}\right)^{2}f_{\rm O}\ M_{\odot}. $$

If the 6364 Å component is only marginally optically thick, this limit decreases by roughly the doublet ratio.

We estimate $v_{\rm O}$ using two different methods: first, a double-Gaussian decomposition of the [O I] $\lambda\lambda 6300,6364$ profile, and second, the half-width at half-maximum intensity measured from the red wing of the 6364 Å line. The second method may suffer from residual H $\alpha$ absorption and dust formation, whereas the first can be affected by line blending along the blue wing. These two approaches yield characteristic velocities of $\sim 4000~\rm km\,s^{-1}$ and $5900~\rm km\,s^{-1}$ , respectively, corresponding to $M^{\rm thick}_{\rm O}>455\,f_{\rm O}\,M_{\odot}$ and $M_{\rm O}^{\rm thick}>1459\,f_{\rm O}\,M_{\odot}$ .

For oxygen masses typical of ordinary CCSNe ( $M_{\rm O}\approx 1\,M_{\odot}$ ; A. Jerkstrand et al. 145, A. Jerkstrand et al. 146, A. Jerkstrand et al. 144, M. Ergon & C. Fransson 89), the doublet remains optically thick only for $f_{\rm O}\lesssim 0.002$ at $v_{\rm O}=4000~\rm km\,s^{-1}$ , or $f_{\rm O}\lesssim 0.0007$ at $v_{\rm O}=5900~\rm km\,s^{-1}$ . For the oxygen masses predicted by H-rich PISN models suitable to explain SN 2023iop’s early light curve ( $M_{\rm O}\approx 50\,M_{\odot}$ ; Table 3; L. Dessart et al. 81), the corresponding requirements are $f_{\rm O}\lesssim 0.11$ and $f_{\rm O}\lesssim 0.03$ .

For comparison, hydrodynamic simulations show that Rayleigh-Taylor instabilities and nickel-bubble expansion fragment the metal core into dense, high-velocity clumps [123]. Nebular spectral modeling of magnetar-powered SNe requires the most extreme clumping, $f_{\rm O}\lesssim 0.01$ , reflecting the strongly compressed inner ejecta produced by sustained central energy injection [149], whereas modeling of ordinary CCSNe adopts $f_{\rm O}\approx 0.01$ –0.1 [145, 146, 144, 89]. By contrast, hydrodynamic simulations of pair-instability explosions find negligible mixing, with no significant redistribution of 56Ni and hence no nickel-bubble-driven clumping [50], so that 1D models reproduce the ejecta structure well [150, 316]. Such largely unmixed ejecta imply comparatively high filling factors, $f_{\rm O}\gtrsim 0.1$ .

### V.3 Stable [Ni II] $\lambda$ 7378

*Figure 12: Emergence of the red component of the 7300 Å complex. Continuum-subtracted profiles on days +99.9 and +326, shown in velocity space relative to [Ca II] $\lambda$ 7291. The blue halves are indistinguishable, and the profiles diverge only redward of $\sim+1000~\rm km\,s^{-1}$ . A distinct second maximum, absent at day +99.9, appears near $+2600~\rm km\,s^{-1}$ at day +326. We attribute it to stable [Ni II] $\lambda$ 7378, blueshifted by $\sim 900~\rm km\,s^{-1}$ (Section V.3).*

Figure 12 compares the [Ca II] region around 7300 Å on days +99.9 and +326. The blue side of the line complex remains unchanged between the two epochs. Both profiles rise identically from $-5000~\rm km\,s^{-1}$ to the peak near the [Ca II] $\lambda$ 7291 rest velocity and begin to diverge only redward of $\sim 1000~\rm km\,s^{-1}$ . By day +326, a distinct emission component has emerged near $+2600~\rm km\,s^{-1}$ that is absent at day +99.9.

This feature is unlikely to be [Ca II] $\lambda$ 7324 from material on the far side of the SN. Such material would contribute to both components of the doublet. Its [Ca II] $\lambda$ 7291 emission would appear at approximately $+1300~\rm km\,s^{-1}$ , nearly coincident with the expected position of [Ca II] $\lambda$ 7324 ( $+1333~\rm km\,s^{-1}$ ). However, the observed profile exhibits a local minimum at this velocity and shows no excess flux relative to day +99.9.

At day +326, [Ca II] is one of the nebular features least affected by radiative-transfer effects. In models of late-time core-collapse SN ejecta, the [Ca II] doublet becomes effectively transparent at an early stage, with its emission tracing the full ejecta volume to within a few percent [301]. Although that model assumes a lower ejecta mass than expected for SN 2023iop (Sections V.1.1, V.4), it also adopts a lower expansion velocity, such that the ejecta densities may not differ substantially. Unlike transitions at shorter wavelengths, [Ca II] should sample the receding hemisphere nearly as effectively as the approaching one.

No other feature in the day +326 spectrum shows a comparable double-horn structure. [O I] $\lambda$ 5577, [O I] $\lambda\lambda$ 6300, 6364 and O I $\lambda$ 7774 are all single-peaked at widths comparable to [Ca II] (Figure 8), and some share the $\sim 1000~\rm km\,s^{-1}$ blueshift noted above. This suggests that the red horn is unlikely to arise from calcium. [Ni II] $\lambda$ 7378, arising from stable 58Ni, provides a more plausible identification. It lies at $+3551~\rm km\,s^{-1}$ relative to [Ca II] $\lambda$ 7291, so the observed peak corresponds to a blueshift of $\sim 900~\rm km\,s^{-1}$ , which is similar to the blueshifted component observed in, e.g., H $\alpha$ and the O I features.

To estimate the luminosity of the red horn, we aligned the blue flanks of the continuum-subtracted line profiles at days +99.9 and +326 and subtracted the earlier spectrum from the later one. Integrating the residual flux between $+1000$ and $+5000~\rm km\,s^{-1}$ yields $\sim 10^{-16}~{\rm erg\,s^{-1}\,cm^{-2}}$ , corresponding to a luminosity of $\sim 3\times 10^{39}~{\rm erg\,s^{-1}}$ . The uncertainty is dominated by the absolute flux calibration and is estimated to be at the level of several tens of percent.

The critical electron density of [Ni II] $\lambda$ 7378 is $\sim 1.5\times 10^{6}~{\rm cm^{-3}}$ [19], above which the level populations approach local thermodynamic equilibrium. At 400 days, electron densities at the core reach $10^{7}$ – $10^{8}~{\rm cm^{-3}}$ in PISN models [147] but only $\sim 10^{6}~{\rm cm^{-3}}$ in ordinary core-collapse SN models [19]. LTE is a reasonable approximation for the PISN scenario, but not for the core-collapse SN one. In either scenario, [Ni II] $\lambda$ 7378 should be optically thin by $\gtrsim 400$ days after explosion according to the aforementioned PISN and CCSN models. In the optically thin LTE limit, the [Ni II] $\lambda$ 7378 luminosity is given (through e.g., equation 42 in A. Jerkstrand 143) by

$$ L_{7378}\approx\left(\frac{M_{\rm Ni\,II}}{0.1~M_{\odot}}\right)\frac{\exp(-19500~{\rm K}/T)}{Z(T)}\times 10^{43}~{\rm erg\,s^{-1}}, $$

where $Z(T)$ is the partition function and $T$ the gas temperature. The observed luminosity implies $M_{\rm Ni\,II}\approx 0.017~M_{\odot}$ at $T=5000$ K, a temperature typical of massive PISN models (see e.g., figure 5 in A. Jerkstrand et al. 147), and $\approx 0.17~M_{\odot}$ at $T=3000$ K.

Stable nickel yields of a few $\times 10^{-2}~M_{\odot}$ are reached in the PISN grid of A. Heger & S. E. Woosley [126] for helium-core masses of $100~M_{\odot}$ and above. Model grids [173, 319, 91] and observations [3, 148, 280, 19] of ordinary core-collapse explosions synthesize a few $\times 10^{-3}~M_{\odot}$ of 58Ni, an order of magnitude less. The core-collapse supernova interpretation is further disfavored because LTE is unlikely to hold at these lower densities, making Equation 11 a strict lower limit on the required nickel mass. The temperature and yield constraints reinforce one another. The higher temperatures of massive PISN models lower the required nickel mass to a value those models supply. The cooler core-collapse models raise it beyond anything they produce.

At later epochs, the temperature in the Ca-rich zones in PISN models is found (see e.g., figure 5 in A. Jerkstrand et al. 147) to be $\sim$ 1000 K lower than in the Ni-rich zones ( $T_{\mathrm{Ni}}\sim$ 5000 K for He130 model and $T_{\mathrm{Ni}}\sim$ 4000 K for He100 model)77 7 Models in the grid of A. Heger & S. E. Woosley [126] are labeled by the mass of the bare helium core in solar masses, so He100 and He130 denote cores of $100$ and $130~M_{\odot}$ .. With almost the same temperature dependence ( $L_{\mathrm{[Ca\,II]}}\propto\exp(-19700\,\mathrm{K}/T)$ ), one then expects $L_{[\mathrm{Ni\,II}]}$ / $L_{[\mathrm{Ca\,II}]}$ to increase by a factor $\sim$ 3 – 5 (for He130 and He100, respectively) compared to early times, where the higher and more similar zone temperatures likely lead to comparable exponentials. This explains the absence/weaker contribution of [Ni II] in the early spectrum, and its arrival in the late spectrum.

Section V.4.1 shows that a hydrogen-rich pair-instability model of a $190~M_{\odot}$ star, R190NL88 8 The L. Dessart et al. [81] model is labeled by zero-age main-sequence mass rather than by core mass, with R190NL denoting a red-supergiant progenitor of $190~M_{\odot}$ ., reproduces SN 2023iop’s early light curve and spectra. Its oxygen core mass of $\sim 79~M_{\odot}$ is almost identical to that of the He100 model. Because stable 58Ni is synthesized in the innermost burning layers, the two models are expected to produce comparable amounts, despite their somewhat different 56Ni yields ( $\sim 2.6$ and $\sim 5~M_{\odot}$ , respectively). The stable nickel mass inferred above is comfortably within the range expected for R190NL. If SN 2023iop is a PISN, the late-time luminosity excess must have a separate origin, with circumstellar interaction as a leading candidate (Section V.4.2).

If correct, identifying the red horn as [Ni II] $\lambda$ 7378 would provide direct evidence for the production of a substantial mass of stable nickel, strongly supporting a PISN interpretation of SN 2023iop. However, this interpretation presently rests on a single spectral feature. Confirmation will require either detecting additional [Ni II] transitions, which would require NIR/MIR observations at late times, or dedicated nebular radiative-transfer modeling tailored to SN 2023iop.

### V.4 Light-curve Modeling

#### V.4.1 Pair-instability Supernova Scenario

We now turn our attention to the light-curve modeling. The broad, luminous light curve is a hallmark of PISN models. We compare the observations of SN 2023iop with PISN models of H-rich stars with a zero age main-sequence mass of $190~M_{\odot}$ from L. Dessart et al. [81] that are based on the calculations of A. Heger & S. E. Woosley [126]. The properties of the blue- and red-supergiant progenitors (B190NL and R190NL), differing in the mass of the H envelope, are summarized in Table 3. These models assume zero metallicity (i.e., a Population-III star) and include nonlocal energy deposition (i.e., $\gamma$ -ray transport). Using the publicly available models99 9 https://zenodo.org/records/5524918, we compute the light curves in the ZTF $g$ , $r$ , and $i$ bands at the redshift of SN 2023iop.

Up until 150 days after peak brightness (Figure 13, top panels), the R190NL model provides a very good match to both the rise and peak luminosity of SN 2023iop, whereas B190NL is systematically $\sim 0.5$ mag fainter at peak in all bands.
