At later phases, however, the agreement breaks down completely. Beyond $\sim 200$ days, the R190NL model follows the expected 56Co decay rate, declining at $\sim 1$ mag per 100 days. In contrast, SN 2023iop fades much more slowly, by merely $\approx 0.2$ mag per 100 days (Section IV.2). By day +326, the discrepancy reaches $\sim 3.5$ mag in $g$ , 1.7 mag in $r$ , and $\sim 0.7$ mag in $i$ . Such a slow decline and blue excess are incompatible with a purely radioactively powered PISN, in which the luminosity directly tracks the exponentially declining energy deposition from 56Co.

The spectral evolution reinforces this conclusion. By day +326, the R190NL model has transitioned to a red, nebular phase, as expected once the ejecta become optically thin. In stark contrast, SN 2023iop remains blue and distinctly photospheric, with strong H $\alpha$ emission. This behavior cannot be reconciled with this PISN model, which predicts a transition to the nebular phase on comparable timescales. The continued presence of a photosphere and strong H emission naturally explains the excess flux in the $g$ and $r$ bands and points to an additional energy source beyond radioactive decay, which we discuss in the next section.

The PISN models used here were computed in the absence of circumstellar interaction, even though their progenitors can lose several tens of $M_{\odot}$ before explosion (Table 3). A late-time excess has also been reported for the H-poor PISN candidate SN 2018ibb [260] and the H-rich candidate SN 2023vbw [131]. In both cases, it was attributed to CSM interaction rather than taken as evidence against a PISN origin. The excesses differ in spectral shape between these objects, so we draw no direct analogy. A suite of PISN models that include ejecta-CSM interaction would be needed to establish whether the excess in SN 2023iop could arise within the PISN channel.

#### V.4.2 Late-time Emission

We used two descriptions of the late-time excess to model and better understand the origin of the late-time behavior of SN 2023iop. The first is a deliberately phenomenological fit to the $gri$ photometry, shown in Figure 14. We fit the light curve in two stages with Redback. First, we establish a baseline at late times by tackling the first peak, fitting it with a radioactive-decay and recombination model [207] via SNmix [253] and sampling the posterior via Bilby [15]. Thereafter, we use this baseline as a prior and add a blackbody component, that we then fit to the $gri$ photometry.

We stress that this analysis is deliberately simple. We are not inferring both components together but using the physically well-motivated radioactive component to anchor the extra phenomenological component. The additional component begins at $269.7$ rest-frame days after the $r$ -band peak and reaches its maximum at $295.8$ days. At that maximum, its effective luminosity, temperature, and radius are $8.2\times 10^{41}~{\rm erg\,s^{-1}}$ , 8500 K, and $4.7\times 10^{14}$ cm, respectively. These quantities describe the timing and color of the excess, but should not be interpreted as measurements of a real blackbody component. As highlighted by the spectrum (Figure 5), the observed late-time SED is not well described by a blackbody. Nevertheless, it helps set some rough constraints to understand what the emission component could be.

The late-time light curve shares several characteristics with the light curve near peak, including a sudden drop in brightness (Figure 2). Such a “replay” could occur if interstellar or circumstellar dust scatters supernova light from an earlier epoch back into the line of sight [57]. If SN 2023iop originates from an extremely massive progenitor, a scattering screen from substantial pre-explosion mass loss is not a contrived scenario. In fact, a light echo was discovered in the H-poor SLSN iPTF16eh [175].

*Figure 14: Two-stage phenomenological modeling of the $gri$ light curves. The photometry is plotted with the indicated magnitude offsets. Dashed curves show the radioactive-decay and recombination baseline, while solid curves denote the baseline plus the additive blackbody component. The latter describes the timing and color dependence of the late excess and is not interpreted as a physical blackbody.*

To test this quantitatively, we model the observed late-time spectrum as a combination of the residual PISN-model spectrum and a rescaled, dust-scattered copy of the near-peak spectrum,

$$ f_{\rm late}(\lambda)=f_{\rm floor}(\lambda)+a\,f_{\rm incident}(\lambda)\,S\!\left(\frac{\lambda}{1+z},\theta\right), $$

where $f_{\rm late}$ is the observed late-time spectrum, $f_{\rm incident}$ is the near-peak spectrum being scattered, $S(\lambda,\theta)$ is a tabulated Milky Way dust-scattering function [288], $\theta$ is the scattering angle, $f_{\rm floor}$ is the late-time PISN spectrum from L. Dessart et al. [81] shown in Figure 13, $a$ is a scaling factor, and $z$ is the redshift of SN 2023iop.

This model reproduces SN 2023iop’s late-time brightness and color reasonably well. The scattering angle has no significant impact on the shape of the spectrum, but only affects the absolute flux level, which the scaling factor $a$ absorbs. However, the fitted spectrum shows a clear mismatch to the data. SN 2023iop’s spectroscopic evolution also remains smooth throughout, with no discontinuity of the kind a light echo would produce, replaying the spectrum at maximum light [244]. This is best seen in H $\beta$ , whose velocity declines smoothly from $\sim 5900~\rm km\,s^{-1}$ near maximum light to $\sim 4100~\rm km\,s^{-1}$ at day +326. This gradual change is also evident in the overall spectral similarity between days +139.8 and +326, despite the $\sim$ 186-day gap separating them (Figure 5). We therefore rule out a light echo as the origin of SN 2023iop’s late-time emission.

Interpreting the expanding blackbody component in the context of CSM interaction is also challenging. Producing such a hot, quasithermal component at large radii would require finely tuned conditions, and it is difficult to reconcile this scenario with the lack of clear spectroscopic signatures of interaction (e.g., narrow Balmer emission lines). While weak or geometrically confined interaction cannot be excluded a priori [280], invoking it in this context appears contrived. Furthermore, the inferred temperature is higher than typically expected for emission associated with dust or reprocessed radiation. This skepticism is reinforced by comparison with SN 2021irp, a luminous, long-lived Type II SN whose excess luminosity and $\sim 0.8$ % continuum polarization have been attributed to interaction with aspherical, disk-like CSM of mass $\gtrsim 2\,M_{\odot}$ [246, 245]. Unlike SN 2023iop, however, SN 2021irp shows clear interaction signatures, including narrow P Cygni components, an Fe II pseudocontinuum, and a lack of absorption lines. The absence of any such features in SN 2023iop’s spectra suggests that, if CSM interaction contributes to its late-time emission, the interacting material must be more deeply hidden than in SN 2021irp.

Given the difficulty of identifying the origin of the emission spectroscopically or via photometry, we instead explore a different question, whether CSM interaction is viable even at a bolometric level. We first construct a restricted pseudobolometric light curve directly from the 24 flux-calibrated, Milky-Way-extinction-corrected spectra. We integrated each spectrum over the common observer-frame interval $4650$ – $9000$ Å (rest-frame $4220$ – $8168$ Å), spanning phases from $-52$ to $+380$ days. We use this reconstruction of the bolometric luminosity rather than from the photometry as it better highlights the late-time plateau and excess, and it can be more easily restricted to energy over a specific wavelength range.

*Figure 15: Joint modeling of the spectroscopic pseudobolometric light curve. Panel A shows the luminosity integrated over the common observer-frame interval $4650$ – $9000$ Å (black points). The solid curve and shaded region are the median and 68% posterior-predictive interval of the radioactive-decay plus CSM model. Dashed and dotted curves represent the median radioactive-decay/recombination and interaction contributions, respectively, after both have been mapped into the observed interval by the same $f_{\rm opt}(t)$ . Panel B shows the median and 68% interval of this single time-dependent optical fraction.*

We fitted these luminosities jointly with a radioactive-decay/recombination component as above and the interaction power generated by the SN ejecta interacting with a static CSM density profile redback-csm [254]. The CSM density was represented by a static 24-node penalized spline to provide maximum flexibility in CSM structure, but we stress that the priors are built to target a smooth power-law density profile. We then assume that only a time-dependent fraction $f_{\rm opt}(t)$ , of the radioactive and interaction power is visible in the $4650$ – $9000$ Å range. A low floor plus a Gaussian enhancement was adopted for this fraction, allowing the optical share to be small at both early and late phases, and largest near the optical peak. The 56Ni mass was restricted to $<5~M_{\odot}$ , motivated by the pair instability models. We assume a conservative 0.10 dex luminosity uncertainty in the likelihood. The data, posterior-predictive light curve, component decomposition, and inferred optical fraction are shown in Figure 15.

This model reproduces the restricted pseudobolometric light curve with small scatter. The inferred ejecta mass is $60^{+43}_{-22}~M_{\odot}$ , the kinetic energy is $18^{+12}_{-8}\times 10^{51}$ erg, and the nickel mass is $3.1^{+1.5}_{-1.7}~M_{\odot}$ (median and 68% credible interval). The corresponding characteristic velocity is $5370^{+640}_{-510}~\rm km\,s^{-1}$ . The spherical-equivalent CSM mass is much less tightly constrained, $7^{+20}_{-5}~M_{\odot}$ , because it is strongly degenerate with the radiative efficiency, which we constrain to $0.24^{+0.22}_{-0.13}$ , and with the fraction of the luminosity emerging in the fitted wavelength interval. The inferred CSM occupies radii of $\sim 10^{16}$ to $7\times 10^{16}$ cm. The fraction of the total luminosity emerging in optical rises from a floor of $0.05^{+0.02}_{-0.03}$ to $0.36\pm 0.09$ near $+13^{+22}_{-21}$ days, with a characteristic width of $58^{+14}_{-9}$ days.

The SN parameters in the joint fit are broadly compatible with the energetic and nickel-rich explosion suggested by the R190NL PISN comparison ( $E_{\rm kin}=33.2\times 10^{51}$ erg and $M_{\rm Ni}=2.6~M_{\odot}$ ), although the ejecta mass is substantially lower than that of the R190NL model ( $164~M_{\odot}$ ; Table 3). This difference could be driven by the uncertain explosion epoch as well as systematic uncertainty and/or different assumptions in our modeling, such as differences in density structure and opacity.

We note that the calculation above assumes a spherical system. For an equatorial band with half-opening angle $\theta$ , a useful first-order conversion is $f_{\Omega}=\Omega/(4\pi)=\sin\theta$ . Holding the radial density fixed within the occupied solid angle gives $M_{\rm CSM,true}\approx f_{\Omega}M_{\rm CSM,sph}$ and $\epsilon_{\rm fit}\approx f_{\Omega}\epsilon_{\rm int}$ . The $30^{\circ}$ – $50^{\circ}$ half-opening angle inferred for the disk-like CSM of SN 2021irp [246, 245] would thus turn our median spherical-equivalent mass into $\sim 3.3$ – $5.0~M_{\odot}$ , while requiring an intrinsic conversion efficiency of $\sim 0.32$ –0.48. These scalings are illustrative because changing the geometry also changes the shock dynamics, optical depth, viewing-angle dependence, and emergent spectrum. Likewise, if a smaller fraction of the interaction power lies in our restricted optical interval than inferred here, more bolometric shock power — and generally more CSM at fixed efficiency — is required. The change is not linear because CSM mass, efficiency, and spectral redistribution are covariant.

The red color near peak brightness (Section IV.2) independently disfavors a dominant early interaction component, although our joint fit was not explicitly forced to make the early CSM luminosity vanish and cannot predict colors because it uses a single $f_{\rm opt}(t)$ . At late times, the absence of narrow lines or other unambiguous interaction signatures (Sections IV.2, IV.4.2) requires any interaction to be hidden, optically thick, geometrically confined, or sufficiently kinematically broadened. The continuum polarization (Section IV.5) makes a nonspherical configuration plausible. Moreover, the absence of a significant change in the optical-NIR colors across the rapid decline (Section IV.2) argues against newly formed dust being its principal cause. A finite equatorial CSM structure, analogous in broad geometry to that proposed for SN 2021irp but spectroscopically more deeply buried, could instead produce a long interaction-powered phase followed by a rapid decline when the shock reaches its outer edge. Two-dimensional radiation-hydrodynamic simulations of ejecta colliding with a circumstellar disk show that the dissipation is concentrated where the ejecta reach the disk rather than in the surrounding wind [290]. A tenuous wind would then be shocked too weakly to produce narrow lines, and the disk emission would emerge only once the overlying ejecta become optically thin. The present light-curve fit shows that such a scenario is energetically viable, and the configuration above offers a route to the absence of spectral signatures, though neither establishes the geometry.

#### V.4.3 Fallback Accretion Powering

We next consider whether fallback accretion onto a central compact remnant can account for SN 2023iop’s light curve. In this scenario, the initial explosion fails to unbind the star. A substantial fraction of the stellar material then falls back onto the newly formed compact object, and the accretion energy released at the center powers the observed emission [83, 202].

We follow the approach of T. J. Moriya et al. [202], who applied it to the extreme 87A-like SN OGLE-73, by using their 40 and 60 $M_{\odot}$ progenitors. Light curves are computed with the one-dimensional (1D) radiation-hydrodynamics code STELLA [30, 29, 31], with the accretion power deposited as thermal energy just above the mass cut. The models contain no 56Ni, so the entire light curve, including the tail, is powered by fallback accretion alone. In the models investigated here, an initial thermal energy $E_{\rm in}=3\times 10^{50}~\mathrm{erg}$ is released at the stellar center. Following the initial energy input, the fallback accretion energy $\dot{E}_{\rm acc}$ is injected from the center as

$$ \dot{E}_{\rm acc}=\eta\,\dot{M}\,c^{2}, $$

where $\eta$ is an efficiency for converting the accretion energy to thermal energy, $\dot{M}(t)$ is the accretion rate which asymptotically approaches $\dot{M}\propto t^{-5/3}$ , and $c$ is the speed of light. The accretion efficiencies are adjusted to match the luminosity of SN 2023iop, and are $\eta=4\times 10^{-3}$ ( $40\,M_{\odot}$ ) and $\eta=5\times 10^{-3}$ ( $60\,M_{\odot}$ ).

Figure 16 compares SN 2023iop’s $ugri$ light curves with the two models. Both reproduce the broad morphology of the observation. The rise lasts more than 100 days, and the tail fades slowly without any radioactive contribution. They fail, however, in two respects.

First, the abrupt decline at the end of the recombination phase occurs too early and is far too sharp. The models drop at day $\sim+30$ ( $40\,M_{\odot}$ ) and day $\sim+60$ ( $60\,M_{\odot}$ ). SN 2023iop instead steepens gradually from day $\sim+50$ onward, with no comparable discontinuity. The mismatch is most severe in the blue, where the model $u$ and $g$ light curves fall by several magnitudes across the transition. T. J. Moriya et al. [202] encountered the same behavior for OGLE-73. They attributed it to the heating source being purely central. Recombination in the H-rich envelope terminates abruptly, and the photosphere then recedes rapidly.

Outward leakage of accretion energy through collimated ejecta would smooth this transition, as would outward mixing of 56Ni. Neither is included in the models. Our $u$ -band limit constrains both. Any process that delays the rapid recession of the photosphere keeps the emergent spectrum blue longer. It therefore raises the predicted $u$ -band flux at the epoch probed by our nondetection. Smoothing the transition enough to match the observed decline would push the models above that limit.

*Figure 16: Comparison of SN 2023iop’s $ugri$ light curves (detections $\bullet$ ; nondetections $\blacktriangledown$ ) with fallback-accretion-powered models for progenitors of $40\,M_{\odot}$ (solid) and $60\,M_{\odot}$ (dashed). The models contain no 56Ni, so the entire light curve, including the tail, is powered by accretion onto the central remnant. Both models reproduce the extended rise and the luminous maximum, but the abrupt decline at the end of the recombination phase occurs earlier and more sharply than observed, most conspicuously in $u$ and $g$ . At late times the $40\,M_{\odot}$ model is too bright in all bands by a band-dependent amount, while the $60\,M_{\odot}$ model is too faint in $g$ and too bright in $i$ , indicating that the predicted colors, and not merely the luminosity scale, disagree with the data.*

Second, the models do not reproduce the observed late-time colors. The $40\,M_{\odot}$ model is too bright at late times in every band, but by a band-dependent amount. The $60\,M_{\odot}$ model is simultaneously too faint in $g$ and too bright in $i$ . The accretion efficiency $\eta$ scales the bolometric output without altering the emergent SED. Adjusting $\eta$ could therefore absorb a uniform luminosity offset, but not a color mismatch. The multiband comparison provides a constraint that the $r$ -band light curve alone does not.

The models also fade smoothly at late times and do not reproduce the sharp decline observed from day $\sim+325$ (Section IV.2). T. J. Moriya et al. [202] noted that energy released at the center may eventually push back the infalling material and suppress the accretion. The light curve would then fade faster than the models predict. They invoked this effect to account for a possible late decline in OGLE-73 near day $+400$ . An abrupt late fade is therefore a predicted feature of the scenario, even though the models computed here do not capture it.

Fallback accretion in this spherically symmetric, centrally heated form thus does not provide a satisfactory description of SN 2023iop. Our $u$ -band limit constrains the two remedies usually invoked for the sharpness of the recombination drop. Departures from spherical symmetry remain a possible escape route. A spread of line-of-sight transition epochs might smear the drop while raising the blue flux less than a uniform smoothing would, though we cannot test this with the available models. We therefore regard fallback accretion as disfavored rather than excluded.

### V.5 Comparison with H-rich SLSNe

Owing to its peak absolute magnitude of $M_{r}\approx-20.14$ mag (Table 1), SN 2023iop also belongs to the broader class of H-rich SLSNe. Most display narrow (a few hundred $~\rm km\,s^{-1}$ ) or intermediate-width ( $\sim 1100~\rm km\,s^{-1}$ ) H $\alpha$ profiles, generally attributed to ongoing interaction between the ejecta and dense CSM [111, 201]. T. Kangas et al. [152] found that only a small fraction of H-rich SLSNe instead show broad Balmer lines ( $>5000~\rm km\,s^{-1}$ ). SN 2023iop, with its broad and persistently regular Balmer P-Cygni profiles (Section IV.4.2), belongs to this rarer subgroup.

*Figure 17: Rest-frame absolute $g$ -band light curve of SN 2023iop (black) compared with the 14 H-rich SLSNe with broad H $\alpha$ from ZTF [152, gray;], spanning $z=0.057$ –0.40. SN 2023iop is the faintest object at peak ( $M_{g}\approx-19.8$ mag), yet it has one of the broadest light curves. Highlighted is SN 2020hgr that is photometrically similar but spectroscopically different from SN 2023iop. Horizontal error bars on SN 2023iop reflect the width of its photometric time bins.*

To place SN 2023iop in this context, we compare its rest-frame $g$ -band light curve with the ZTF broad-H $\alpha$ SLSN II sample of T. Kangas et al. [152] (Figure 17). Two features stand out. First, with a peak absolute magnitude of $M_{g,\rm peak}\approx-19.8$ mag, SN 2023iop is the faintest object in the comparison. Second, its light-curve width places it at the opposite extreme of the distribution. Its half-flux rise time is $t_{1/2,\rm rise}>36$ rest-frame days,1010 10 T. Kangas et al. [152] reported only the rise time from 50% peak flux for their sample. We therefore measured the light-curve parameters of the comparison objects using the same method as for SN 2023iop. The resulting 50%-flux rise times agree with those reported by T. Kangas et al. [152]. a lower limit because the $g$ -band monitoring began well after explosion, later than the first $r$ -band observation. The well-sampled $r$ -band light curve gives $t_{1/2,\rm rise}=75$ rest-frame days (Table 1). Because the $g$ - and $r$ -band peaks are separated by only 12.6 rest-frame days, small compared with the rise timescale itself, the true $g$ -band rise time is expected to be comparable, and thus longer than that of any object in the T. Kangas et al. [152] sample. Its half-flux decline time, $t_{1/2,\rm decline}\approx 66$ rest-frame days, is roughly twice the sample median of $\sim 34$ days, and essentially tied with the longest in the sample, SN 2020yue ( $\sim 66.5$ days). SN 2023iop is therefore not a scaled-down version of a typical SLSN II.

The closest photometric analog within the broad-line sample is SN 2020hgr [152], also the slowest-evolving object. Its early-time light curve resembles that of SN 2023iop near maximum brightness, but its published coverage is limited to phases around peak brightness, precluding any comparison with SN 2023iop’s extended plateau and slow spectroscopic evolution (Sections IV.4.2, V.6.1). Despite their photometric similarity, the two objects differ spectroscopically. SN 2020hgr exhibits a persistent UV excess and an anomalously weak H $\alpha$ absorption component, which led T. Kangas et al. [152] to conclude that it is an interaction-powered event. SN 2023iop shows neither signature. Its $u$ -band and Swift/UVOT photometry reveal no UV excess at peak (Section IV.2), and its H $\alpha$ profile retains a strong, regular P-Cygni absorption trough throughout the photospheric phase (Section IV.4.3). A further difference emerges in the strength of forbidden emission lines at late times. Such lines are essentially absent across the broad-line SLSN II sample of T. Kangas et al. [152]. Even the weak forbidden emission lines reported in SN 2020hgr remain far weaker than the well-developed [Ca II] $\lambda\lambda 7291$ ,7324 and [O I] $\lambda\lambda 6300$ ,6364 emission that strengthens in SN 2023iop from day $+135.3$ onward (Section IV.4.2). The single broad-line SLSN with a comparable light curve therefore appears to be powered differently from SN 2023iop.

SN 2023iop is thus doubly unusual. It belongs to the rare broad-line tail of the H-rich SLSN population, and even within that tail its combination of luminosity, rise time, and late-time spectral behavior has no close counterpart. Together with the comparison to the 87A-like population in Section V.6, this places SN 2023iop at the extreme end of the 87A-like class in both luminosity and timescale. Its SLSN classification, by contrast, follows from peak luminosity alone and does not carry the interaction-powered origin that characterizes most events of that class.

### V.6 Comparison with Other SN 1987A-like Objects

SN 2023iop’s light curve is reminiscent of the Type II SN 1987A. To place SN 2023iop in context, we compare its light curve and spectra with those of regular 87A-like SNe and with the small set of previously identified extreme 87A-like events. As a reference, we use the volume-limited sample of 87A-like SNe from the ZTF Census of the Local Universe survey [70, 272], with ZTF light curves from Miller et al. (in prep.) and spectra from A. Singh et al. [270] and T. Sit et al. [272] retrieved from WISeREP. We also include SN 1987A itself, whose photometry and spectroscopy [124, 241] are likewise available on WISeREP. To extend the comparison toward the most luminous events, we add the extreme 87A-like SNe OGLE-73 [295] and 2020faa [324, 251]. Although not formally an 87A-like SN, we also include the extraordinary Type II SN iPTF14hls [10, 279] as a further point of comparison.

All light curves and spectra were corrected for Milky Way extinction and, where applicable, for host-galaxy attenuation. For nearby objects such as SNe 1987A and 2018hna, redshift-based distance estimates are unreliable. We instead adopt the distance moduli from G. Pietrzyński et al. [231] and I. D. Karachentsev et al. [153], respectively. For each object, we derive characteristic light-curve properties following the methodology outlined in Section IV.2.

Recently, D. Hiramatsu et al. [131] reported a further extreme 87A-like event, SN 2023vbw ( $M_{\rm peak}\approx-19.2$ mag), which they interpret as a pair-instability explosion. It is $\sim 0.9$ mag fainter at peak than SN 2023iop and radiated $3\times 10^{50}$ erg, so SN 2023iop remains the most luminous and most energetic member of the class. A detailed comparison of the two events is deferred to Skoglund et al. (in prep.) and does not affect the conclusions drawn here.

#### V.6.1 Light Curve

Figure 18 compares the $r$ -band absolute-magnitude light curve of SN 2023iop with those of the comparison sample. With $M_{r}=-20.1$ mag (Table 4), SN 2023iop is the most luminous object in the sample by a substantial margin: it exceeds the peak luminosities of OGLE-73 ( $M_{R}=-19.2$ mag) and SN 2020faa ( $M_{r}=-18.9$ mag), the most luminous extreme 87A-like SNe known previously, by $\sim 0.9$ and $1.3$ mag, respectively. Regular 87A-like events span $M\approx-15.6$ to $-17.4$ mag, so SN 2023iop outshines objects such as SN 2018hna ( $M_{r}=-16.2$ mag) and SN 1987A ( $M_{R}\approx-16.5$ mag) by $\sim 3.7$ –4.0 mag, not only at peak brightness but throughout most of its evolution.

The rest-frame $(g-r)_{0}$ color of SN 2023iop at $r$ maximum, measured from the spectrum on day $+13.6$ , is $g-r=0.44$ mag. The same procedure yields $g-r=0.36$ mag for SN 2020faa ( $-8$ days) and $g-r=0.33$ mag for OGLE-73 ( $-16.1$ days; Table 4). Since H-rich SNe cool and redden after maximum brightness, these pre-maximum measurements are likely somewhat bluer than the true peak colors. For comparison, SN 1987A had $g-r\approx 1.08$ mag at maximum light, while SN 2018hna reached $g-r\approx 0.59$ mag ( $-9.6$ days). The color of SN 2023iop thus lies between the regular and extreme 87A-like subclasses.

The post-maximum evolution reveals a qualitative distinction between the regular and extreme 87A-like events. Regular objects decline from peak light and settle onto a linear (in magnitudes) tail consistent with the 56Co $\to^{56}$ Fe decay rate of $0.98$ mag (100 day)-1, as exemplified by SNe 1987A and 2018hna. In contrast, SNe 2020faa and 2023iop first decline gradually to $\sim$ 50% of their peak flux and then drop much more rapidly. Between the epochs of $1/e$ and $1/10$ peak flux, the decline rates are $2.6$ mag (100 day)-1 for SN 2023iop, $3.4$ mag (100 day)-1 for OGLE-73, and $8.8$ mag (100 day)-1 for SN 2020faa. No regular 87A-like SN shows such a steep drop. It resembles instead the end of the recombination phase in Type IIP SNe [327, e.g.,], although the preceding light curves are concave (87A-like) rather than plateau-like. After the drop, however, the light curves of SN 2023iop and SN 2020faa flatten again and fade far more slowly than 56Co decay would allow (SN 2023iop: $0.2~{\rm mag\,(100~day)^{-1}}$ ; Section IV.2).

At $\sim 376$ days after peak light, the brightness of SN 2023iop dropped sharply by 3 mag (100 day)-1 (Section IV.2), a behavior without counterpart among the regular 87A-like SNe. Whether OGLE-73 and SN 2020faa did the same is unknown, as neither was observed at these epochs. A comparably rapid late-time drop, following an extended slow-decline phase, has been observed in the CSM-interaction-powered luminous Type II SN 2021irp, which steepened to $2.7$ mag (100 day)-1 after $\sim 250$ days [246]. There, the transition was attributed to either a sharp decrease in the CSM-interaction power or the onset of dust formation and reprocessing [246].

A further intriguing comparison object is the peculiar Type II SN iPTF14hls [10, 279]. Although not formally classified as an 87A-like event, its early photometric evolution closely resembles that of the extreme 87A-like SNe OGLE-73, 2020faa, and 2023iop (Figure 18). All four objects exhibit unusually broad light curves and long diffusion timescales compared to ordinary SNe II, pointing to exceptionally massive H-rich ejecta, an additional energy source, or both. The later evolution tells a different story. While SNe 2023iop and 2020faa, and likely OGLE-73, decline relatively rapidly after the end of their broad maximum-light phase, iPTF14hls maintained a high luminosity for several hundred days and rebrightened repeatedly [10, 279]. A possible interpretation is that the early-time similarity reflects a shared ejecta configuration, a massive H envelope with a long diffusion timescale, while a second parameter governs the late-time evolution, for instance the strength and duration of central-engine activity [75], fallback accretion [202], or CSM interaction [8]. iPTF14hls and the extreme 87A-like events would then be neighbors in a broader family of massive H-rich explosions rather than products of a single explosion or progenitor channel.

#### V.6.2 Spectrum

Figure 19 compares the spectral evolution of SN 2023iop with that of regular and extreme 87A-like SNe. All spectra were scaled to the same continuum level between 5500 and 6200 Å (rest frame), enabling a direct comparison of the continuum shapes and the relative strengths of the absorption and emission features. Near maximum light, all objects show the characteristic appearance of a Type II SN, with broad Balmer P-Cygni profiles superposed on a blue continuum. Nevertheless, clear differences separate the regular and extreme members of the class. The spectra of OGLE-73, SN 2020faa, and SN 2023iop are systematically bluer than those of SNe 1987A and 2018hna, indicating higher photospheric temperatures, reduced line blanketing by iron-group elements, or both.

In addition, the metal absorption features, particularly those of Fe-group species, are noticeably weaker and less distinct in the extreme 87A-like objects (Section V.6.3). Their spectra appear smoother, with absorption troughs that are both shallower and more heavily blended, consistent with the larger expansion velocities of the extreme events (see below). A further difference is the systematically lower H $\alpha$ absorption-to-emission ratio in OGLE-73, SN 2020faa, and SN 2023iop compared to SNe 1987A and 2018hna. In all of these respects, the extreme events differ from their regular counterparts, and SN 2023iop sits firmly within the extreme group.

The clearest difference is the pace of the spectral evolution. By $\sim 100$ days after maximum light, SNe 1987A and 2018hna have already developed conspicuous nebular features, including strong [Ca II] emission and a markedly strengthened H $\alpha$ emission component [241, 270]. In contrast, SN 2023iop remains largely photospheric at comparable epochs, with persistent Balmer and Fe II P-Cygni profiles and only weak signs of a transition toward the nebular phase. OGLE-73 and SN 2020faa occupy an intermediate regime, evolving more slowly than regular 87A-like SNe but more rapidly than SN 2023iop. The spectroscopic sequence mirrors the photometric one (Section V.6.1). Both point to a continuum of progressively longer diffusion and recombination timescales, plausibly set by the mass of the H envelope [328, 81, 240].

By $\sim 330$ days (Figure 19, panel C), the contrast has widened further. SNe 1987A and 2018hna are fully nebular by then, and their spectra are dominated by strong, relatively narrow emission lines with little underlying continuum. SN 2023iop instead retains a well-defined continuum with only weak [O I], [Ca II], and Ca II NIR emission, and its H $\alpha$ emission is $\sim 50\%$ weaker than in the regular 87A-like events. Nearly 1 yr after maximum light, SN 2023iop has therefore not yet reached the state that SN 1987A attained within $\sim 100$ days. iPTF14hls evolved even more slowly, remaining largely photospheric at a comparable phase.

*Figure 20: Evolution of the Fe II $\lambda$ 5018 photospheric velocity of SN 2023iop compared with 87A-like SNe and iPTF14hls. The regular events (SNe 1987A and 2018hna) reach higher velocities at early phases but decelerate rapidly. The more luminous events evolve more slowly and retain higher velocities at comparable phases, consistent with more massive ejecta slowing the inward recession of the photosphere in velocity space. iPTF14hls is a clear outlier; it holds a nearly constant $\sim 4000~\rm km\,s^{-1}$ for more than 400 days despite being far less luminous than the extreme 87A-like events, so its flat velocity evolution does not follow the same luminosity trend.*

The slow spectral evolution is also reflected in the velocities. Figure 20 shows that the photospheric velocity inferred from Fe II $\lambda$ 5018 declines rapidly in the regular 87A-like SNe, whereas the evolution is substantially slower in the more luminous events. SN 2023iop exhibits the most gradual velocity evolution in the sample, maintaining comparatively high velocities at phases when SNe 1987A and 2018hna have already decelerated significantly. Similar behavior has been noted for OGLE-73 and SN 2020faa [295, 324]. It is expected if the extreme objects carry more massive ejecta, because the photosphere then recedes more slowly in velocity space and the nebular phase begins later [12, 81, 240, 239].

While the velocity evolution points toward unusually massive ejecta, the spectropolarimetry constrains their geometry. The continuum polarization of $P\approx 0.8$ –1.0% measured on day +37 shows that the photosphere departed significantly from spherical symmetry at an epoch when ordinary SNe II are essentially unpolarized (Section IV.5).

#### V.6.3 Metallicity

L. Dessart et al. [82] showed that the EW of Fe II $\lambda$ 5018 can serve as a proxy for the natal iron abundance and hence for the metallicity of the progenitor at the time of its formation. To compare the absorption strengths at a common epoch, we measured the EW of Fe II $\lambda$ 5018 at a photospheric temperature of 6000 K, adopting the temperature evolution from I. Arcavi et al. [11], G. Terreran et al. [295], A. Singh et al. [270], and I. Salmaso et al. [251], together with our measurements from Section IV.3.

The resulting rest-frame EWs define the following sequence, from lowest to highest: OGLE-73 ( $6.0\pm 0.5$ Å), SN 2018hna ( $7\pm 1$ Å), SN 2023iop ( $8\pm 1$ Å), SN 1987A ( $13\pm 1$ Å), and SN 2020faa ( $16\pm 4$ Å). iPTF14hls spans a broader range of $10$ – $20$ Å [11, taken from], overlapping with the upper half of this sequence. All of these values are substantially lower than that of SN 2023ixf [271, 35–40 Å; taken from], which exploded in a solar-metallicity environment [307]. This suggests that the 87A-like events in our comparison sample span a range of metal-poor environments, with SN 2018hna, SN 2023iop, and OGLE-73 occupying the lowest-metallicity end.

To place SN 2023iop on an absolute metallicity scale, we compiled oxygen-abundance measurements of H II regions near the sites of SNe 1987A, 2018hna, 2020faa, iPTF14hls, and OGLE-73 [189, 11, 295, 270, 324]. These studies find metallicities of $\sim 0.1$ – $0.6~Z_{\odot}$ , following the same ordering as the Fe II $\lambda$ 5018 EWs. This correspondence indicates that the progenitor of SN 2023iop formed in a markedly metal-poor environment. Section IV.7 presents an independent, host-mass-based metallicity estimate for SN 2023iop.

Reduced line-driven mass loss at low metallicity allows stars to retain more-massive H envelopes until core collapse [275, 310], providing a plausible physical link between these metal-poor environments and SN 2023iop’s observed properties.

#### V.6.4 Host Galaxies

*Figure 22: Host galaxy of SN 2023iop shown in the context of hosts of 87A-like SNe from the volume-limited ZTF Census of the Local Universe survey, together with SN 1987A and the two extreme 87A-like events OGLE-73 and SN 2020faa, and regular SN II from the Palomar Transient Factory (66, 90, 95%-ile contours). The gray band indicates the star-formation-rate vs. stellar-mass relation for star-forming galaxies. Supernova host galaxy studies have proven to be powerful tools for constraining SN progenitor populations [174, 168, 113, 226, 53, 294, 229]. To place the host of SN 2023iop into context, we compare it with hosts of 87A-like SNe from the volume-limited ZTF Census of the Local Universe survey [272] and with the extreme 87A-like events OGLE-73 and SN 2020faa (Figure 22). We also compare these systems with the host-galaxy population of ordinary SNe II from the Palomar Transient Factory study of S. Schulze et al. [259]. The hosts of regular 87A-like SNe broadly overlap with the ordinary SN II host distribution, covering the mass range of sub-SMC [192, $4.6\times 10^{8}~M_{\odot}$ ;] and MW-like galaxies [172, $6\times 10^{10}~M_{\odot}$ ;]. The extreme 87A-like events, however, occupy its low-mass tail. The host galaxy of iPTF14hls falls in the same low-mass region, considerably less massive than the typical hosts of nearby SNe II.

With a stellar mass of only $\sim 10^{8.2}\,M_{\odot}$ , the host of SN 2023iop is among the least massive galaxies in our comparison sample. It is more than two orders of magnitude less massive than the median host of the known 87A-like population. It is also a factor of 30 less massive than the common hosts of nearby SNe II [259]. Through the galaxy mass–metallicity relation [299], this low mass implies a significantly lower progenitor metallicity than typically inferred for ordinary SNe II. Those SNe predominantly occur in approximately solar-metallicity environments [259]. This independent, mass-based estimate is consistent with the spectroscopic and nebular metallicity constraints presented in Section V.6.3.

Although the current sample remains small, the emerging picture is that extreme 87A-like events preferentially occur in metal-poor host galaxies, and that metallicity plays an important role in shaping their properties. As argued in Section V.6.3, reduced mass loss in such environments would let massive stars retain more of their H envelope until core collapse, which could explain the defining traits discussed in Sections V.6.1 and V.6.2, including broad light curves, slow velocity evolution, and delayed transition to the nebular phase.

Taken together, this evidence places SN 2023iop at an even more extreme end of the 87A-like parameter space than OGLE-73 and SN 2020faa, with a higher luminosity and longer characteristic timescales than either object. However, it remains unclear whether the regular and extreme 87A-like events form a single physical sequence or merely occupy a similar region of observational parameter space. One possibility is that the 87A-like light-curve morphology can arise from multiple channels, including explosions that differ substantially in progenitor structure and powering mechanism. In this context, iPTF14hls is particularly interesting: although it shares several properties with the extreme 87A-like events during the first few hundred days, its subsequent evolution suggests that additional physical ingredients, such as prolonged central-engine activity or CSM interaction, may play an important role [8, 314, 318, 279, e.g.,].

### V.7 A Multiwavelength Roadmap for Extreme 87A-like Supernovae

The growing sample of extreme 87A-like events includes objects with very similar early-time photometric and spectroscopic properties but potentially different physical origins. Pair-instability explosions, central-engine activity, fallback accretion, and hidden CSM interaction can all reproduce broad light curves and long-lived photospheric spectra, so the power source cannot be inferred from optical data alone. The most discriminating diagnostics may instead arise in the UV, IR, radio, or X-rays, on timescales ranging from days after explosion (shock breakout, UV excess) to years (dust formation, CSM interaction, radio transparency, accretion-powered X-rays). Below we outline observational tests for each scenario. They are primarily intended for newly discovered extreme 87A-like events that future surveys will find, but some of them can still be applied to SN 2023iop.

The importance of such diagnostics is illustrated by SN 2023iop itself. Its luminosity plateau followed by a rapid decline would remain undetected in individual Rubin/LSST images1212 12 https://rubinobservatory.org/for-scientists/rubin-101/key-numbers at $z\gtrsim 0.3$ (single-image depths: $g\approx 24.5$ , $r\approx 24.0$ , $i\approx 23.4$ , $z\approx 22.9$ mag), or in James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) transient surveys beyond $z\gtrsim 2$ at COSMOS-like depths [102, $m_{\rm lim}\approx 28$ mag;] and $z\gtrsim 6$ even in JADES [73, $m_{\rm lim}\approx 30$ mag;]. At such distances, SN 2023iop would be classified as a PISN candidate from its peak luminosity, rise time, and early spectra alone. If it is not a PISN, such misclassifications would bias inferred PISN rates across cosmic time [39, 107], with ramifications for massive-star and galaxy evolution [126, 125] and the interpretation of the LIGO black-hole mass function [1, 296].

#### (i) PISN Diagnostics

PISNe are most directly identified through their exceptionally large iron-group yields, best probed in the nebular phase. The thermonuclear disruption of very massive helium cores synthesizes up to tens of solar masses of 56Ni, and once the ejecta turn optically thin the spectra should be dominated by neutral and low-ionization emission from intermediate-mass elements (Si I, S I, Ca I–II) and iron-group elements ([Fe II–III], [Co II], [Ni II]), whose integrated luminosities trace the iron-group mass, its distribution, and mixing [147]. At $\gtrsim 1~\rm yr$ , cooling shifts to the NIR, producing prominent 2–5 $\mu$ m features [147] analogous to those seen in Type Ia SNe [162, 32]. JWST/NIRSpec [140, 1–5 $\mu$ m;] and MIRI [315, 5–28 $\mu$ m;] cover these features over a wide redshift range. Since core-collapse explosions yield $\ll 0.5~M_{\odot}$ of iron-group material and only rarely $\sim 1~M_{\odot}$ [5, 293, 282], the strength of these features cleanly separates the two channels. Their absence would argue against a PISN origin.

Dust provides a complementary test. PISN models predict $\sim 1$ – $30~M_{\odot}$ of dust ( $\sim 15$ –30% of the progenitor mass), mainly silicates and oxides, forming within a few years [257]. These predicted dust masses exceed those inferred for nearby core-collapse SNe, typically $\sim 0.01$ – $1~M_{\odot}$ , by one to several orders of magnitude [188, 291, 267, 287]. The predicted yields are upper limits and are sensitive to mixing, molecule formation, and reverse-shock destruction. Nevertheless, dust masses $\gtrsim 1\,M_{\odot}$ at $\gtrsim 100~\rm K$ are readily detectable with MIRI in the not-so-distant Universe, providing an unambiguous discriminator against core-collapse or magnetar-powered explosions [217, 118, 54].

Early-time UV observations offer another test. Radiation-hydrodynamic calculations predict exceptionally luminous shock-breakout flashes from H-rich PISNe [158, 157, 49, for a review, see]. These flashes peak in the extreme UV and soft X-rays, reach luminosities of $\sim 10^{45}$ – $10^{46}~\rm erg~s^{-1}$ , and last for several hours in the progenitor rest frame. They are substantially more luminous than the shock-breakout emission expected from ordinary core-collapse SNe. High-cadence UV facilities such as ULTRASAT [269] and UVEX [161] could therefore directly test a pair-instability origin.

#### (ii) Magnetar Diagnostics

Whereas the PISN scenario is primarily constrained through its nucleosynthetic products and radioactive-energy deposition, models powered by a compact remnant are more naturally tested through signatures of prolonged energy injection into the ejecta. Sustained magnetar input maintains high ionization in the inner ejecta and enhances the excitation of Ne, Ar, and S, whose strongest transitions lie in the IR. The [Ne II] 12.8 $\mu$ m fine-structure line is predicted to be the brightest MIR feature, with $L\approx 10^{39}$ – $10^{40}\,\rm erg\,s^{-1}$ in magnetar-powered SNe, and its strength is set by the magnetic field, spin-down timescale, and ejecta mass, making it a direct probe of the central engine [215, 76, 214]. It is not expected to be prominent in purely radioactive explosions, where ionization is lower, and energy deposition is confined to iron-group-rich regions [147]. MIRI Medium Resolution Spectroscopy [315, MRS;] is uniquely suited to detect this line in nearby PISN-like transients. However, MIRI/MRS is split into four channels, and Channel 4 ( $\lambda>17.98\,\mu\rm m$ ) is significantly less sensitive than Channels 1–3; redshifting [Ne II] 12.8 $\mu\rm m$ into Channel 4 imposes an effective redshift limit of $z\approx 0.4$ for this diagnostic method. Combined with NIRSpec and optical nebular data, its detection or absence discriminates between magnetar, radioactive, and interaction powering.

A magnetar also predicts a secondary, engine-driven shock breakout. The inflated high-pressure bubble drives a radiative shock through the ejecta that emerges days after explosion as a UV/optical transient with luminosities of $\sim 10^{43}$ – $10^{44}~\rm erg~s^{-1}$ and durations of several days [155, 51]. It may appear as a distinct first peak or as a short-lived UV excess preceding the main light-curve maximum. High-cadence UV monitoring is therefore among the most direct probes of central-engine activity.

#### (iii) Fallback Accretion Diagnostics

Fallback accretion resembles magnetar-powered models but distinctively predicts long-lived emission from the accretion flow, whose luminosity tracks $\dot{M}\propto t^{-5/3}$ [58] or an advection-dominated plateau [83] independent of the environment. An interaction luminosity instead follows the CSM density profile. A steady wind ( $\rho_{\rm csm}\propto r^{-2}$ ) gives $L_{\rm X}\propto t^{-1}$ [137], whereas shells and density cutoffs imprint abrupt rebrightenings or drops [59, 87, 308, 180].

Detecting the accretion flow is difficult. The engine lies beneath the ejecta, where its emission is absorbed by the K-shell electrons of the metals [4]. Hydrogen and helium contribute little at these energies, and a fallback explosion ejects little iron, so the opacity per unit mass falls well below that of the metal-rich compositions for which it is usually computed. Scaling the relation of I. Andreoni et al. [7] to our ejecta masses therefore overestimates the optical depth. Even so, only emission above $\sim 10$ –30 keV escapes within the first few years, while the soft band stays opaque for decades. Because an advection-dominated flow carries most of its energy inward rather than radiating it, fallback models predict only $L_{\rm X}\approx 10^{39}~\rm erg\,s^{-1}$ [83, 202], so even a NuSTAR-class detection would require an event within $\sim 10$ Mpc. An external shock can also be heavily absorbed early, but by its own CSM, whose column falls rapidly as the shock overruns it [48, 120]. Soft X-rays therefore emerge within months for an interacting SN and only after decades for a buried engine.

Radio observations are more promising, though the same competition applies. Free-free absorption scales steeply with frequency and time ( $\tau_{\rm ff}\propto\nu^{-2.1}\,t^{-5}$ ; P. G. Mezger & A. P. Henderson 197, K. Murase et al. 203, B. Margalit et al. 179, C. M. B. Omand et al. 216), so the dense, still-ionized ejecta clear from high frequencies downward. For $M_{\rm ej}=12$ – $60~M_{\odot}$ , they become transparent after $\approx 2$ –4 yr in the ALMA bands [320, 84–950 GHz;] but only after one to two decades at centimeter wavelengths. Early ALMA monitoring is the only route to catching an engine as it emerges, at the cost of observing where a synchrotron spectrum has already declined. For a source as luminous as PTF10hgi [88, 167, $L_{\nu}\lesssim 10^{28}~\rm erg\,s^{-1}\,Hz^{-1}$ at 6 GHz;] with a spectrum falling as $\nu^{-0.7}$ , a deep observation near the transparency epoch reaches $\sim 100$ Mpc, an order of magnitude beyond the hard X-ray test, and further if the self-absorption turnover lies in the millimeter bands. Centimeter facilities instead provide population coverage. The DSA-2000 [122] will image the sky north of $\delta=-30^{\circ}$ every four months at $\sim 2~\mu\rm Jy\,beam^{-1}$ RMS (0.7–2 GHz), and the ngVLA [264, $\lesssim 0.4~\mu\rm Jy\,beam^{-1}$ per hour at $\sim 8$ GHz;] adds multifrequency coverage of the turnover.

Radio emission is less specific, however. Its brightness depends on uncertain jet energetics and microphysics, and CSM interaction [55, 59, 60] or a magnetar-born pulsar-wind nebula [216, 179] can produce comparable luminosities. The spectral turnover helps, since a buried source clears from high frequencies downward whereas an external shock is limited by synchrotron self-absorption [56]. Distinguishing the two engines (i.e., black hole and magnetar) is harder, as both lie behind the same screen. A pulsar-wind nebula is intrinsically radio-bright, radiating from radio to $\gamma$ -rays, whereas an advection-dominated flow radiates poorly and emits in the radio only if it launches a jet. A firmer separation may come from the optical light curve, through an abrupt accretion turn-off [83, 202] or periodic modulation from a companion, as in SN 2022jli [52].

#### (iv) CSM Diagnostics

CSM interaction converts ejecta kinetic energy into radiation at external shocks and can in principle supply both the high peak luminosity and the late-time flux excess. The difficulty lies in its concealment. If the CSM is confined and rapidly engulfed, or the interaction proceeds in a buried disk or torus, the narrow emission lines that define SNe IIn are suppressed, and the light curve alone cannot separate interaction from radioactive or engine powering [276, 211, 251]. Hidden interaction nevertheless leaves subtler imprints. These include narrow ( $\sim 10^{2}~\rm km\,s^{-1}$ ) Balmer features from the unshocked CSM, intermediate-width ( $\sim 10^{3}~\rm km\,s^{-1}$ ) components with electron-scattering wings [63, 135, 103], boxy flat-topped late-time H $\alpha$ from a cold dense shell [8, e.g., iPTF14hls;], and weaker P-Cygni absorption troughs, which occur when continuum light from outside the line-forming region dilutes the absorption feature beneath it [36]. Detecting or excluding these signatures requires $R\gtrsim 5000$ ( $\lesssim 60~\rm km\,s^{-1}$ ) and high S/N, since the features are weak perturbations on a bright continuum.

Interaction also reshapes the SED. The shock sustains a hot continuum that resists the reddening of a recombination-cooled photosphere and produces a persistent blue and UV excess. T. Kangas et al. [152] identified such excesses in some H-rich SLSNe, most notably SN 2020hgr, whose otherwise ordinary SN II spectra show an extremely weak H $\alpha$ absorption component. Together, the UV excess and the diluted absorption identify it as a primarily interaction-powered event despite the absence of narrow SN IIn-like lines. UV and $u$ -band photometry around maximum brightness, combined with the strength of the H $\alpha$ trough, thus tests for hidden interaction even when optical spectra appear unremarkable. This diagnostic also separates interaction from engine powering. An internal engine heats the ejecta below the line-forming layer, so the P-Cygni absorption remains strong, whereas external interaction dilutes the absorption and imprints the CSM velocity field on the line profiles. If optically thick CSM dominates the luminosity, the shock breakout itself is also modified, with a larger breakout radius, a lower effective temperature, and UV emission that lasts days rather than hours and evolves more slowly in color [60, 209, 252, 329].

For SN 2023iop, these CSM tests return negative results. The $u$ -band and Swift/UVOT photometry around maximum light show no UV excess (Section IV.2), and the high-resolution, high-S/N spectra reveal strong, regular H $\alpha$ P-Cygni absorption (Figure 5), in marked contrast to SN 2020hgr, with no narrow or intermediate-width features at any epoch. We find no evidence that CSM interaction dominates during the epochs probed by our optical and UV data. Any interaction scenario for the late-time excess must therefore operate without producing narrow lines or absorption filling. Radio and X-ray observations constrain extended, wind-like material, but a shock confined within the ejecta is screened as effectively as an embedded engine, so nondetections do not exclude it.

Several of these diagnostics will soon be available for SN 2023iop. Approved JWST observations [261] will obtain deep MIRI imaging and spectroscopy, directly testing the pair-instability (dust formation) and magnetar ([Ne II] line) scenarios. In X-rays, our upper limit on the unabsorbed flux ( $<1.2\times 10^{-13}~{\rm erg\,cm^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$ , 0.3–10 keV; corresponding to $L_{\rm X}<4\times 10^{42}~{\rm erg\,s^{-1}}$ at $z=0.1020$ ; Section IV.6) is more than three orders of magnitude above the fiducial fallback-accretion luminosity discussed above, so this test remains inconclusive. Moreover, the ejecta remain optically thick to bound-free absorption across this band at the epoch observed (Section IV.6), so a nondetection is expected regardless of depth.

In the radio, our 15.5 GHz limit ( $L_{\nu}<4.4\times 10^{28}~\rm erg\,s^{-1}\,Hz^{-1}$ ; Section IV.6) lies a factor of $\sim 4$ above the PTF10hgi detection [88]. Given the possibly large ejecta masses and low expansion velocities of extreme 87A-like events, however, the free-free optical depth at centimeter wavelengths remains high for one to two decades [197, 203, 179, 216], so a deeper observation at this frequency would not test an embedded engine. The higher frequencies accessible to ALMA are far less affected (see above) and become transparent within a few years of explosion. SN 2023iop may now be entering the epoch at which such a search becomes feasible. Centimeter monitoring with the VLA and, eventually, systematic coverage with DSA-2000 will supply the long-term light curve once those frequencies clear.

## VI Conclusions

We have presented optical, NIR, UV, radio, X-ray, and spectropolarimetric observations of SN 2023iop, a luminous H-rich SN at $z=0.1020$ . Its broad light curve, slow spectral evolution, and delayed transition toward the nebular phase make it the most extreme 87A-like supernova known. Our main conclusions are as follows.

- • SN 2023iop is the most extreme 87A-like transient currently known. It reached a peak luminosity of $M_{r}\approx-20.1$ mag, $\geq 0.9$ mag brighter than OGLE-73 and SN 2020faa, and exhibited an exceptionally broad light curve with a rise time $\gtrsim 88$ rest-frame days.

- • SN 2023iop’s peak luminosity also places it among the H-rich SLSNe. Broad Balmer lines are rare in that class, and SN 2023iop is one of the few such objects. It is the faintest of them at peak but has one of the broadest light curves, and its well-developed late-time forbidden lines have no counterpart among them. It does not show the interaction signatures that characterize most H-rich SLSNe.

- • Despite its extraordinary luminosity, the optical spectra closely resemble those of regular Type II SNe. However, the spectral evolution is much slower than in both normal SNe II and classical 87A-like events, with strong photospheric features remaining visible several hundred days after maximum light.

- • The combination of broad light curves, slow velocity evolution, delayed nebular transition, and host-galaxy properties points toward an unusually massive H-rich envelope as a key ingredient of SN 2023iop and, possibly, the broader population of extreme 87A-like transients.

- • The light-curve rise of $\gtrsim 88$ rest-frame days implies an ejecta mass of $M_{\rm ej}>12~M_{\odot}$ . The peak luminosity requires $\approx 2.2~M_{\odot}$ of 56Ni, compatible with the tail-based upper limit and with the yield from the joint interaction fit. These numbers exceed the yields attainable in neutrino-driven explosions, but both the peak- and tail-based values assume radioactive decay dominates the luminosity, and are therefore upper limits.

- • An emission feature emerging near 7300 Å after day +140 is tentatively identified as [Ni II] $\lambda$ 7378 from stable 58Ni. The implied mass of $\approx 0.02~M_{\odot}$ is reached only in the most massive PISN models and exceeds ordinary core-collapse supernova yields by an order of magnitude. For the 58Ni/56Ni ratios of $\approx 0.01$ –0.02 predicted by these models, it corresponds to $\approx 1$ – $2~M_{\odot}$ of 56Ni, consistent with the light curve modeling.

- • The continuum polarization of 0.8–1.0% measured on day +37.3 indicates a substantial departure from spherical symmetry at the photospheric phase.

- • The host galaxy is a low-mass dwarf system, placing SN 2023iop within the metal-poor tail of the SN II host-galaxy population. Together with OGLE-73, SN 2020faa, and iPTF14hls, this suggests that metallicity may play a role in producing the most slowly evolving H-rich explosions. A metal-poor environment is also a prerequisite for the pair-instability channel [165], since retaining a helium core of $\gtrsim 65~M_{\odot}$ requires weak line-driven winds.

- • Existing H-rich pair-instability models reproduce much of the early light-curve evolution but not the prolonged photospheric phase or the late-time luminosity, whose excess is most pronounced in the blue. These models are computed without any interaction between the ejecta and the material their progenitors are expected to shed. Hidden, geometrically confined interaction could supply the missing energy without producing the narrow lines that are absent from the spectra at every epoch. The late-time mismatch therefore does not by itself exclude a pair-instability origin.

- • Fallback accretion reproduces the broad light-curve morphology but does not match late-time colors, and our $u$ -band limit constrains the modifications that would otherwise smooth its recombination transition. A light echo is excluded by the smooth spectroscopic evolution.

- • More broadly, SN 2023iop demonstrates that markedly different physical mechanisms can produce similar optical observables. The extreme 87A-like events therefore need not share a common powering mechanism. Pair-instability explosions, hidden circumstellar interaction, and central-engine activity may all occur within the population, and SN 2023iop itself appears to require more than one of them.

- • The features that identify SN 2023iop as unusual are the first to be lost with distance. Its late-time plateau and subsequent rapid decline lie below the single-image depth of Rubin/LSST beyond $z\approx 0.3$ , and below JWST survey limits beyond $z\approx 2$ –6, leaving only the peak luminosity, rise time, and early spectra, from which SN 2023iop would be classified as a PISN candidate without reservation. Yet it is the late-time data that reveal a plateau no powering mechanism reproduces and that require an additional energy source. Distant PISN candidates will therefore appear cleaner than they are, biasing the PISN rate inferred across cosmic time and the constraints that rate places on massive-star evolution and on the black-hole mass function.

The high 56Ni mass, the large ejecta mass, and the metal-poor host each point toward a very massive progenitor, and the tentative detection of stable nickel strengthens that case. We consider a pair-instability explosion the most plausible interpretation of SN 2023iop. In that case, the late-time excess must come from an additional energy source, most likely circumstellar interaction. The identification of the nickel line rests on a single feature, however, and needs independent confirmation. It also remains unclear whether the extreme 87A-like events are a continuous extension of the classical population or a distinct class of H-rich explosions. Answering these questions requires a larger sample with comparably comprehensive coverage and the multiwavelength diagnostics outlined in Section V.7: early UV coverage of the shock breakout, MIR searches for dust and fine-structure lines, and radio and X-ray monitoring of the putative engine. For SN 2023iop itself, the approved JWST observations will provide the first of these tests.

## Appendix A Observations and Data Reduction

### A.1 Photometry

#### A.1.1 Observations with All-sky Surveys

#### Asteroid Terrestrial-impact Last Alert System (ATLAS)

ATLAS is a network of robotic 0.5 m $f/2$ Wright-Schmidt telescopes designed for rapid, all-sky monitoring [297]. During the period relevant to this work, ATLAS operated sites at Haleakalā and Mauna Loa (Hawaii, USA), Sutherland (South Africa), and El Sauce (Chile), providing coverage of both hemispheres.

Each ATLAS unit has a field of view of $\sim 30~\mathrm{deg}^{2}$ . Observations are obtained using two custom broad optical filters: cyan ( $c$ ; $\sim 4200$ –6500 Å) and orange ( $o$ ; $\sim 5600$ –8200 Å; J. L. Tonry et al. 297). Individual exposures are 30 s in duration, typically reaching a $5\sigma$ limits of $\sim 19.5$ –19.8 mag (AB) under dark conditions. The ATLAS survey strategy prioritises cadence over depth. Each field is generally observed multiple times per night, with revisit times on the order of 30–60 min, and the full accessible sky is typically covered every 1–2 nights [297].

ATLAS data are processed using an automated reduction and image-subtraction pipeline, including photometric and astrometric calibration against external reference catalogues, described by B. Stalder et al. [283]. We ran the ATLAS Forced Photometry service1313 13 https://fallingstar-data.com/forcedphot [268] on all relevant images. The data were clipped and binned using the Python script plot_atlas_fp.py1414 14 https://gist.github.com/thespacedoctor/86777fa5a9567b7939e8d84fd8cf6a76. We used a bin size of 2 days for all data. Measurements with a significance of $<3\sigma$ were removed from the final light curve.

#### 40 cm Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer

The field of SN 2023iop was also observed during the Near-Earth Object Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer (NEOWISE) all-sky MIR survey, the reactivation mission of the WISE space telescope, in the $W1$ (3.4 $\mu$ m) and $W2$ (4.6 $\mu$ m) bands [322, 178]. We retrieved time-resolved coadded images of the field created as part of the unWISE project [163, 196].

#### Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF)

ZTF is a wide-field optical survey operating on the 1.2 m Samuel Oschin Schmidt Telescope at the Palomar Observatory (California, USA). ZTF is operated as a public-private partnership, combining a public time-domain survey with a suite of private and collaboration-led programs. The telescope is equipped with a 600-megapixel mosaic camera covering $47~\mathrm{deg}^{2}$ [74], enabling rapid synoptic coverage of the northern sky [21].

Observations were performed in the ZTF $g$ and $r$ bands as part of the public survey, with additional $i$ -band imaging obtained through a private survey program. Each exposure had a duration of 30 s, reaching a median $5\sigma$ point-source depth of $g\approx 20.6$ mag and $r\approx 20.4$ mag (AB) under nominal conditions [21, 186]. During the 2023–2024 observing seasons, the public survey strategy revisited most extragalactic fields approximately at a two-night cadence.

ZTF data were processed through the real-time image-subtraction pipeline at the Infrared Processing and Analysis Center (IPAC), which performs bias subtraction, flat-fielding, astrometric calibration, and photometric zeropoint determination, followed by image differencing using reference images [186]. Transient candidates are identified on difference images and distributed via public-alert streams [186, 222, 177]. These candidates were vetted and managed using the Fritz Marshal system [66], which is based on the SkyPortal Framework [305].

We reprocessed the ZTF data of SN 2023iop using the ZTF Forced Photometry service [187]. These were cleaned and calibrated as described by [187]. To boost the S/N, we combined same-night observations in each filter.

#### A.1.2 Targeted Observations

#### 8.2 m ESO Very Large Telescope

Between July and October 2024, we obtained photometry in $gRIz$ with the FOcal Reducer/low dispersion Spectrograph 2 [9, FORS2;] at the ESO 8.2 m Very Large Telescope at Paranal Observatory (Chile). These data suffered from progressively increasing contamination by the host galaxy. To remove the host contribution, we took a final set of deep $gRIz$ photometry in June 2025. These reference images were obtained under similar observing conditions, but their integration times were a factor of 2 longer to ensure a reliable host subtraction. We reduced the data with the FORS2 pipeline v5.6.51515 15 https://www.eso.org/sci/software/pipelines/fors and the ESO workflow engine ESOReflex [106]. The world coordinate system was calibrated with the software package astrometry.net [164].

#### 8.4 m Large Binocular Telescope

We performed NIR observations in January 2026 (after the SN had faded below the host level) with the Large Binocular Telescope (LBT), located on Mount Graham (Arizona, USA). The LBT consists of two comounted 8.4 m primary mirrors, providing a large collecting area and excellent image quality. Imaging was obtained using the LUCI instruments (LUCI1 and LUCI2; W. Seifert et al. 263), which provide imaging and spectroscopic capabilities in the NIR. Observations were acquired in the $J$ and $K_{s}$ bands using standard dither patterns to enable accurate sky subtraction. The data were processed using the data-reduction pipeline developed at INAF – Osservatorio Astronomico di Roma [99], which includes bias subtraction and flat-fielding, bad-pixel and cosmic-ray masking, astrometric calibration, sky subtraction, and coaddition. Field stars from the Gaia DR3 catalog [108, 109] were used for astrometric calibration.

#### 2.0 m Liverpool Telescope

The Liverpool Telescope is a fully robotic 2.0 m telescope located at the Observatorio del Roque de los Muchachos on La Palma (Canary Islands, Spain). Between June 2023 and August 2024, optical imaging was performed using the IO:O instrument [284]. Observations were obtained in Sloan-like $g$ , $r$ , $i$ , and $z$ filters. Reduced images were downloaded from the LT archive and processed using a custom image-subtraction and analysis software (K. Hinds, K. Taggart, et al., in prep.). Image stacking and alignment were performed using SWarp [26] where required. Image subtraction was done using a pre-explosion reference image in the appropriate filter from the Pan-STARRS Data Release 1 (DR1) [47]. Photometry was measured using PSF-fitting techniques based on the methods of C. Fremling et al. [105].

#### 6.5 m Magellan Telescope

Optical imaging with the Magellan Baade 6.5 m telescope was obtained using the Inamori-Magellan Areal Camera and Spectrograph (IMACS; A. Dressler et al. 86), located at Las Campanas Observatory, Chile. IMACS was operated in imaging mode with Sloan-like $g$ and $r$ filters. The data were reduced following standard optical imaging procedures, including bias subtraction, flat-field correction, and astrometric calibration.

#### 6.5 m MMT

Late-time photometry was acquired in the $g$ and $r$ bands with Binospec [95] on the 6.5 m MMT telescope at Mount Hopkins (Arizona, USA), as well as in the $J$ band with the MMT and Magellan Infrared Spectrograph [193, MMIRS;]. The data were reduced using the Pipeline for Optical/infrared Telescopes in Python for Reducing Images (POTPyRI)1616 16 https://github.com/CIERA-Transients/POTPyRI, which automatically conducts standard image-reduction procedures including bias subtraction, flat-field correction, and astrometric calibration.

The $g$ - and $r$ -band observations suffered from tracking loss. This led to an elongated and deformed point-spread function. Due to the this, we omit these data from further analysis.

#### Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory

We acquired two epochs with the 30 cm Ultraviolet/Optical Telescope [248, UVOT;] aboard the Swift satellite [115] between 14 and 17 September 2023 in $w2$ , $m2$ , $w1$ , $u$ , $b$ , $v$ . The science-ready data were retrieved from the Swift archive1717 17 https://www.swift.ac.uk/swift_portal. SN 2023iop was not detected in these data. Since the data were taken only 3 days apart and SN 2023iop evolves extremely slowly, we coadded all images in each filter using fappend and uvotimsum in HEAsoft1818 18 https://heasarc.gsfc.nasa.gov/docs/software/heasoft/ version 6.30 [210].

#### 2.56 m Nordic Optical Telescope

The 2.56 m Nordic Optical Telescope (NOT) is located at the Observatorio del Roque de los Muchachos on La Palma, Canary Islands, Spain. Optical imaging was acquired with the Andalucía Faint Object Spectrograph and Camera1919 19 https://www.not.iac.es/instruments/alfosc (ALFOSC), using standard Sloan-like $g$ , $r$ , and $i$ filters, in January and November 2024. Data reduction was performed with PyNOT2020 20 https://github.com/jkrogager/PyNOT, which applies standard procedures, including bias subtraction, flat-field correction, and coadding data. Strong winds, dust, and clouds affected the January observations. In addition, a mismatch between the ALFOSC science images and the VLT template images affects the image subtraction. Therefore, we do not report photometry for those data.

NIR imaging at the NOT was obtained using the NOTCam instrument [85] in the $J$ , $H$ , and $K_{s}$ bands between September 2023 and the end of June 2024. The data were reduced using standard NIR techniques, including dark subtraction, flat-fielding, sky subtraction, and coaddition.

#### Palomar 60-inch Telescope

Additional optical imaging was obtained with the robotic Palomar 60-inch (1.52 m) telescope (P60; S. B. Cenko et al. 45), located at Palomar Observatory (California, USA), using the Spectral Energy Distribution Machine [27, SEDM;] in imaging mode. Images were obtained in Sloan-like $g$ and $r$ . The data were reduced using the data-reduction pipeline FPipe [105].

#### A.1.3 Supernova Photometry

The ZTF and ATLAS forced-photometry light curves were calibrated following F. J. Masci et al. [186] and K. W. Smith et al. [274], respectively. To increase the S/N of the ATLAS data, we combined same-night observations in each filter with inverse-variance weighting, using plot_atlas_fp.py2121 21 https://gist.github.com/thespacedoctor/86777fa5a9567b7939e8d84fd8cf6a76, and imposed an S/N threshold of 5. The ZTF data were combined with a dynamic binning scheme (also using inverse-variance weighting): (1) $\rm min(\Delta t)=1$ day and $\rm min(S/N)=10$ between MJD 60000 and 60100; (2) $\rm min(\Delta t)=1$ day and $\rm min(S/N)=5$ between MJD 60100 and 60300; and (3) $\rm min(\Delta t)=20$ days and $\rm min(S/N)=4$ between MJD 60300 and 60700, where $\Delta t$ is the width of the time bin. The higher S/N threshold in the first interval accounts for the elevated noise of the earliest observations, obtained as part of the ZTF twilight survey [22]. The coarser binning in the third interval is needed to recover SN 2023iop, which is not detected in individual images at late times; the exact choice of binning parameters does not affect the overall shape of the late-time light curve.

Photometry from targeted ground-based optical imaging was extracted with the AutoPhOT pipeline [38]. We first refined the world coordinate system of each image with Astrometry.net [164] and constructed an effective-PSF (ePSF) model from bright, isolated stars using Photutils [35]. Zeropoints were calibrated against stars from the ATLAS All-Sky Stellar Reference Catalog REFCAT2 [298]. Science and reference images were aligned with SWarp [26], and the SN flux was isolated through image subtraction with the saccadic fast Fourier transform algorithm [134, SFFT;]. Whenever SN 2023iop was not detected at the $\geq 3\sigma$ level, we determined the limiting magnitude of the image via artificial-source injection, as detailed by S. J. Brennan & M. Fraser [38].

At the time of the NIR observations with NOTCam, SN 2023iop was several magnitudes brighter than its host galaxy, making host contamination negligible. We therefore measured the SN brightness directly, without image subtraction, using the aperture-photometry tool of S. Schulze et al. [258], which is based on Source Extractor [25]. The instrumental magnitudes were calibrated against stars from the Two Micron All Sky Survey [273, 2MASS;] Point Source Catalog [68], measured in the same way.

For the MMIRS NIR data, we extracted the photometry using a different method for each epoch. For the first epoch, we performed image subtraction with HOTPANTS v5.11 [20], using the LBT image as the reference and measuring the residual flux by aperture photometry. In the second epoch, the image quality was substantially better than that of the LBT reference, so subtraction would have degraded it. We instead recovered the SN flux by forward modeling the science frame, following an approach similar to that of GALFIT [224]. We modeled the image as the sum of a PSF-convolved Sérsic host galaxy, a point source at the fixed transient position, and a constant sky background. An empirical PSF was built for each epoch from unsaturated field stars with Source Extractor [25] and PSFEx [23]. We fitted all model parameters simultaneously by nonlinear least squares and derived the uncertainties from the covariance matrix scaled by the reduced $\chi^{2}$ . The photometry was calibrated with the same stellar sample and PSF model. We regarded any epoch with a point-source flux uncertainty above 50% as unreliable, since such values indicate that the host and transient were not sufficiently resolved.

SN 2023iop is not detected in the UVOT images. We measured the brightness at the position of SN 2023iop with the Swift tool uvotsource, using a source aperture of radius $10^{\prime\prime}$ and a substantially larger background region, and calibrated the photometry with the calibration files from September 2020.

For the MIR data, we performed image subtraction on the NEOWISE images with a custom pipeline [71] based on the ZOGY algorithm [326], using the full-depth coadds from the WISE and NEOWISE missions (obtained during 2010–2014) as reference images. Photometric measurements were then obtained through forced PSF photometry at the position of SN 2023iop on the subtracted images.

Strong spectral features can introduce time-dependent color terms between similar but not identical filters and, if uncorrected, add non-negligible systematic scatter to the light curves [286, e.g.,]. Appendix Figure 23 illustrates this issue: it shows the spectra at $+71.7$ and $+326.0$ days, overlaid with the response curves of the filters used during the follow-up campaign. A comparison of the ZTF $r$ and $i$ bands with the other filters shows that individual filters can either cover or miss particularly strong spectral features. However, since each instrument was used only during a limited time span, over which the spectral features changed little, we can assume a constant color term (also known as $s$ correction) for each instrument.

Where needed, all measurements were converted to the AB system using the offsets from M. R. Blanton & S. Roweis [28], A. A. Breeveld et al. [37], and R. M. Cutri et al. [69].

Appendix Tables 5 and 6 summarize the final photometric measurements. Nondetections are reported as $3\sigma$ upper limits. This table also presents the photometry after applying the $s$ correction and correcting for Milky Way extinction, assuming the J. A. Cardelli et al. [44] attenuation law, a total-to-selective extinction ratio of $R_{V}=3.1$ , and the E. F. Schlafly & D. P. Finkbeiner [256] Milky Way extinction map. The value of the Milky Way extinction along the line of sight of SN 2023iop is $E(B-V)=0.05$ mag. All photometric measurements will also be made available through WISeREP.
