#### A.1.4 Host-galaxy Photometry

After the SN had faded, we observed the SN host galaxy with the ESO VLT and the LBT from the $g$ to the $K$ bands. To measure the galaxy flux and preserve the intrinsic galaxy colors, we selected the deepest image and defined a circular aperture encompassing the entire galaxy. Next, we adjusted the aperture size according to the seeing conditions for each image and measured the brightness using the aforementioned aperture-photometry tool developed by S. Schulze et al. [258]. The photometry was calibrated against stars in the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) DR9 [2] and stars from the 2MASS Point Source Catalog [68]. The NIR measurements were converted to the AB system using the values reported by M. R. Blanton & S. Roweis [28]. The final photometry is listed in Appendix Table 8. These measurements are not corrected for Milky Way extinction, but the correction was applied to all derived measurements reported in this paper.

### A.2 Spectroscopy

#### 8.2 m ESO Very Large Telescope

We acquired two medium-resolution spectra with the X-shooter instrument [309] on 1 November and 2 December 2023 (days +71.7 and +99.9). All observations were performed in nodding mode and with 1 $\farcs$ 0/0 $\farcs$ 9/0 $\farcs$ 9 wide slits (UVB/VIS/NIR). The integration time was 3600 s for each epoch. The data were reduced following J. Selsing et al. [265]. In brief, we first removed cosmic rays with the tool astroscrappy2222 22 https://github.com/astropy/astroscrappy, which is based on the cosmic-ray removal algorithm by P. G. van Dokkum [306]. Afterward, the data were processed with the X-shooter pipeline v3.3.5 and the ESO workflow engine ESOReflex [116, 200]. The UVB and VIS-arm data were reduced in stare mode to boost the S/N. The individual rectified, wavelength-calibrated, and flux-calibrated two-dimensional (2D) spectra files were coadded using tools developed by J. Selsing2323 23 https://github.com/jselsing/XSGRB_reduction_scripts. The NIR data were reduced in nodding mode to ensure good sky-line subtraction. In the third step, we extracted the 1D spectra of each arm in a statistically optimal way using tools by J. Selsing. Finally, the wavelength calibration of all spectra was corrected for barycentric motion. The spectra of the individual arms were stitched by averaging the overlap regions.

We obtained two epochs of late-time spectroscopy with the FOcal Reducer and low-dispersion Spectrograph 2 instrument (days +326.0 and +623.8). Each observation was performed with the 300V grism and a 1 $\farcs$ 0 wide slit. The integration time of each epoch was $12\times 1200$ s. The data were reduced with the reduction pipeline PypeIt [238, 237].

#### 10 m Keck Telescope

We obtained one epoch with the DEep Imaging Multi-Object Spectrograph [94, DEIMOS;] on 7 October 2023 (day +49.5) and another epoch with the Low Resolution Imaging Spectrometer [213, LRIS;] on 17 October 2023 (day +58.4). The DEIMOS observation utilized the low-resolution grating 600ZD, an 0 $\farcs$ 8-wide slit, and the GG455 order-blocking filter. The integration time was set to 900 s. The LRIS spectrum was acquired with the B400/3400 blue-side grism and the R400/8500 red-side grating, dichroic 560, and a 1 $\farcs$ 0-wide slit. The integration time was 1200 s. All spectra were reduced in a standard fashion with the reduction pipeline PypeIt and LPipe [225].

#### 8.4 m Large Binocular Telescope

We also obtained one epoch of spectroscopy on 28 January 2025 (day +483.8) with the Multi-Object Double Spectrographs MODS-1 and MODS-2 [235] mounted on the LBT. The observation consisted of $9\times 1200$ s exposures. ABBA offsets were used in the dual-grating mode (G400L and G670L), providing wavelength coverage 3200–9500 Å and a slit mask with a width of $1\farcs 2$ . We processed the spectral data using the Spectroscopic Interactive Pipeline and Graphical Interface (SIPGI) tool [114], and we applied corrections for bad pixels and cosmic rays, followed by bias subtraction and flat-field correction. The wavelength calibration was calculated from comparison-lamp frames, also to correct for optical distortion. Finally, the wavelength- and flux-calibrated, sky-subtracted 2D spectra were combined, and the 1D spectrum of each source was extracted. The spectra were flux-calibrated using a sensitivity function derived from spectrophotometric standard stars.

#### 2.0 m Liverpool Telescope

We obtained a spectrum with the SPectrograph for the Rapid Acquisition of Transients [230, SPRAT;] at the LT using a blue-optimized setup, which was reduced using a custom python pipeline. This pipeline is based on the packages lacosmic [306], NumPy [304], SciPy [311], and Astropy [16]. Aperture sizes and polynomial fits for sky subtraction and trace fitting were set manually to optimize the S/N. Table 1 from La Palma Technical Note2424 24 https://www.ing.iac.es/Astronomy/observing/manuals/ps/tech_notes/tn031.pdf No. 31 was used to correct for differences in airmass between the science and standard-star frames.

#### 6.5 m Magellan

We obtained a high-resolution spectrum with the Magellan Echellette [182, MagE;] spectrograph mounted on the Magellan Clay Telescope on 21 October 2023 (day +61.7). MagE provides wavelength coverage 3200–10,000 Å and, with the 0 $\farcs$ 85 slit employed for these observations, delivers a spectral resolving power of $R\approx 4800$ . The data were reduced using the PypeIt pipeline.

#### 6.5 m MMT

We obtained optical spectroscopy of SN 2023iop with the Binospec spectrograph [95] mounted on the 6.5 m MMT Observatory. The observations were acquired on 10 and 15 January 2024 (day +135.3 and 139.8) and 5 May 2024 (day +296.2) using the 270 line mm-1 grism with a central wavelength of 6500 Å and a $1^{\prime\prime}$ -wide slit, providing wavelength coverage 3850–9150 Å at a resolving power of $R\approx 1340$ . The data were reduced using PypeIt.

#### 2.56 m Nordic Optical Telescope

We acquired two epochs of low-resolution spectroscopy with ALFOSC on 29 August 2023 and 24 September 2023 (days +13.6 and +37.2). The spectra were obtained with a 1 $\farcs$ 0-wide slit and grism #4. The data were reduced using PypeIt.

#### Palomar 60-inch Telescope

The SED Machine at the Palomar 60-inch Telescope is a very low resolution ( $R\approx 100$ ) integral-field unit covering the wavelength range 3650–10,000 Å [27]. We acquired a series of spectra between 18 June and 16 October 2023 (days $-51.4$ to $+57.4$ ). All data were reduced with HyperGal [170] that uses the output from pysedm [247, 159]. In this paper, we present only the highest-quality spectra for which no other observations are available. All reduced spectra, irrespective of their quality, are available on WISeREP.

#### Remarks

All spectra were calibrated against spectroscopic standard stars observed during the same night, and the flux scale was tied to our multiband photometry. Also, spectra were corrected for Milky Way extinction. A host-attenuation correction was not applied as it is negligible (Section IV.1). The absolute flux-calibrated spectra are available on WISeREP [325].

### A.3 Spectropolarimetry

We obtained one epoch of spectropolarimetry on 24 September 2023 (day +37.3) with VLT/FORS2. The data were reduced using a custom pipeline [317], which extracts ordinary and extraordinary beam spectra optimally within regions of equal size ( $4\times$ FWHM of the ordinary beam). Three cycles of spectra were obtained over the half-wave plate angles $0\fdg 0$ , $22\fdg 5$ , $45\fdg 0$ , and $67\fdg 5$ , and these were combined using inverse-variance weighting.

The observations were taken with a $65\%$ full-moon illumination at an angle of $\sim 87^{\circ}$ from the Moon. The high, scattered lunar background may have influenced the results. We investigated this by measuring the local background level in different regions alongside each beam. Estimating the background level farther away from each beam resulted in more significant polarization increasing toward the blue. When placing the background regions (with a width of 10 pixels, similar to the measurement aperture) right next to the aperture of each beam, the wavelength dependence of the polarization is minimal, and the Moon does not appear to have a significant effect in the presented polarimetry. Regardless, we exclude $<5000$ Å, where the Moon’s influence was strongest, from the analysis.

The spectropolarimetry was calibrated against a standard star. Polarisation bias correction was performed following S. Plaszczynski et al. [233]. In addition, the flux scale of the intensity spectrum was tied to the multiband photometry. A host-attenuation correction was not applied as it is negligible (Section IV.1). The absolute flux-calibrated intensity spectrum is available on WISeREP.

### A.4 Radio Observations

We observed the field of SN 2023iop at radio wavelengths with the Arcminute Microkelvin Imager Large Array [330, 129, AMI-LA;] at the Mullard Radio Astronomy Observatory (United Kingdom) on 15 November 2023 and 5 December 2023, corresponding to 84.4 and 102.6 rest-frame days after $r$ -band peak light, respectively. AMI-LA is a radio interferometer consisting of eight 12.8 m (diameter) antennas, providing 28 baselines ranging from 18 to 110 m and operating over a 5 GHz bandwidth centered at 15.5 GHz.

The data were reduced, flagged, and calibrated using reduce_dc, a customised AMI-LA data-reduction pipeline [227]. Phase calibration was performed using short, interleaved observations. Imaging was carried out with the Common Astronomy Software Applications [194, CASA;] task CLEAN, and the image RMS noise was measured using the CASA task IMSTAT. No source is detected at the position of SN 2023iop down to a flux density of 48 $\mu$ Jy (RMS) at a central frequency of 15.5 GHz.

### A.5 X-ray Observations

While monitoring SN 2023iop with UVOT, Swift also observed the field with its onboard X-ray telescope XRT between 0.3 and 10 keV in photon-counting mode [41]. We analyzed these data with the online tools of the UK Swift team2525 25 https://www.swift.ac.uk/user_objects that use the software package HEASoft version 6.26.1 and methods described by P. A. Evans et al. [92], P. A. Evans et al. [93]. SN 2023iop was not detected at any epoch. As these two epochs were taken within 3 observer-frame days of each other, we combine them to go deeper.

The $3\sigma$ count-rate limit is $3\times 10^{-3}~\rm s^{-1}$ (0.3--10 keV) on day +30.3. To convert this limit into a flux, we assume a power-law spectrum with a photon index2626 26 The photon index is defined as the power-law index of the photon flux density ( $N(E)\propto E^{-\Gamma}$ ). of $\Gamma=2$ and a Galactic neutral hydrogen column density of $3.91\times 10^{20}$ cm-2 [128]. The count-rate limit translates to an unabsorbed flux of $<1.2\times 10^{-13}~{\rm erg\,cm}^{-2}\,{\rm s}^{-1}$ in the range 0.3–10 keV.

## Appendix B Host Galaxies of 87A-like Supernovae

T. Sit et al. [272] reported 13 long-rising Type II SNe from the volume-limited Census of the Local Universe survey. These authors gave some host properties, but not the host photometry. Following the methodology of S. Schulze et al. [259], we retrieved the science-ready images from the Galaxy Evolution Explorer (GALEX) general release 6/7 [183], the SDSS DR 9 [2]), the Pan-STARRS DR1 [47], the 2MASS [273], and reprocessed WISE images from the unWISE archive [163]. The unWISE images include data from the NEOWISE Reactivation mission [178, 195] through Year 6/7. The optical photometry was complemented by images from the DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys [84, Legacy Surveys, LS;] DR10, where data were missing. We measured the host brightness using LAMBDAR [321, Lambda Adaptive Multi-Band Deblending Algorithm in R;] and utilized tools developed by S. Schulze et al. [259]. This sample was complemented with two luminous 87A-like SNe (OGLE-73, G. Terreran et al. 295; SN 2020faa, S. Yang et al. 324). The photometry of the OGLE object was measured from Legacy Survey images, and the photometry of SN 2020faa and iPTF14hls were taken from S. Yang et al. [324] and S. Schulze et al. [259], which also employed the methods from S. Schulze et al. [259]. All measurements are summarized in Table 9 in the Appendix.

## Abstract

Photometric classifiers decide which of the million nightly alerts of time-domain surveys receive one of the few thousand spectra taken each year, and they are the first place where a transient outside the trained classes can be noticed. We present flare, the photometric classification and anomaly-detection module of AppleCiDEr, evaluated on $10\,497$ spectroscopically confirmed ZTF transients in six classes and $53$ objects from families outside the taxonomy. Catalogue context raises the macro $F_{1}$ score, with the largest gains where the defining information is absent from the light curve. Blind detection recovers few out-of-taxonomy objects at a $1\%$ false-alarm rate, while a simulated review loop recovers $83\%$ of them after inspecting $15\%$ of the stream. The first confirmations of a new family are most useful in the feature space: with the same eleven labels, a head on the frozen features detects $68\%$ of the tidal disruption events hidden from the training against $57\%$ for a combiner over the anomaly scores, and retraining with them as a new class reaches $85\%$ . The module runs in production on Fritz, the ZTF instance of SkyPortal, and its alarm is reported as a false-alarm rate per unit time on the stream, calibrated on the photometry that the service receives.

#### Keywords:

## I Introduction

Since the start of its operations in 2018, the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF; 6, 23, 14) has distributed up to about a million alerts per night [48], and the Vera C. Rubin Observatory [33], which began distributing alerts in February 2026, is expected to reach about ten million per night once the survey is fully operational. Only a few thousand of these transients are classified spectroscopically each year, so that photometric classifiers decide, in practice, which alerts receive a spectrum, and they are also the first place where a new kind of transient can be noticed, as an object that matches none of the trained classes.

So far, several photometric classifiers have been developed for this task [47, 17, 53, 65], and many of them run today inside the alert brokers [57, 46, 45, 34]. Anomaly searches have used light-curve features [43], expert feedback [42, 32] and the latent space of a trained classifier [49, 26]. These tools address successive stages of discovery, in which an unfamiliar object is flagged, confirmed by a human and finally represented by a trained class, and in this work we compare the three stages on the same objects, with the aim of measuring how the first confirmations of a new family should be used.

A second question concerns the information available to each stage. Some class distinctions depend on the luminosity or on the position within the host galaxy, which public catalogues can supply at the time of the alert, while others depend on spectral features. For this reason, we interpret the errors of the classifier and the recovery of the anomalies in terms of these observables, and we measure the contribution of each block of catalogue context; the models themselves are empirical, and the physics enters through the organisation of the analysis.

Here, we introduce flare, the photometric module of the AppleCiDEr framework [36], which is built for the boom alert broker [34] and whose spectroscopic module, astraNet, provides classifications, anomaly scores and prediction sets for spectra [54, 70]. flare uses the ZTF photometry and public catalogues, without spectra or image cutouts, and we evaluate it on $10\,497$ spectroscopically confirmed transients and on $53$ objects from families outside its six-class taxonomy.

We focus on three aspects of this workflow: (i) the information that the external context adds to the light curve (Section IV); (ii) the recovery of the out-of-taxonomy objects by blind ranking, active review and learning from the first labels (Sections V and VI); and (iii) the reliability of both layers under missing context, short observation horizons and the transfer to the sources of Fritz (Sections VII–IX). Finally, we discuss the limitations in Section X and present our conclusions in Section XI.

## II Benchmark

### II.1 Spectroscopically confirmed sample

The labels come from the ZTF Bright Transient Survey [18, 50, BTS;], a magnitude-limited catalogue in which $12\,916$ of $20\,547$ objects have a spectroscopic type; we impose no cut beyond its peak limit of $19$ . The classified fraction is $81\%$ for objects brighter than $18.5$ and $41\%$ for fainter ones, so that the $7\,631$ unclassified objects are on average half a magnitude fainter (Section X). The catalogue carries the selection function of the survey: BTS saves extragalactic candidates, so that the $304$ cataclysmic variables (CVs) and $251$ active galactic nuclei (AGN) of the benchmark are the members of these classes that most resembled supernovae, a harder set than the raw stream, and tidal disruption events (TDEs) enter by the same route, while dedicated photometric searches recover them more completely [60].

We retrieve the ZTF photometry [44] of each object through the boom broker [34], and we require at least eight detections, with at least two in each of the $g$ and $r$ bands, within a $100$ -day window from the first detection; the $i$ band is used where present, but it is absent from the public alert stream and contributes $1.2\%$ of the detections, so that we describe the light curves as two-band. In total, $10\,497$ objects of the six trained classes and $52$ of families outside the taxonomy pass these criteria, and we add AT 2018cow (ZTF18abcfcoo), the prototypical fast blue optical transient, which passes every cut but is listed as “other” in the catalogue; the out-of-taxonomy hold-out thus contains $53$ objects, and the benchmark $10\,550$ .

The six trained classes are a coarsening of the taxonomy of the companion spectroscopic classifier astraNet [54], in which its Ibc and II classes are merged into a single core-collapse class, so that the spectroscopic probabilities map onto the photometric classes by summation and the two predictions can be combined. The families of the hold-out play the role of the unknown classes in this work (Section V.1).

### II.2 What a light curve carries, class by class

For the interpretation of the following sections, we summarise for each class the property that distinguishes it and whether a two-band light curve can measure it. The shape and the colour evolution identify most Type Ia supernovae, while the stripped-envelope core-collapse supernovae can resemble them at the ZTF cadence and are separated by spectral lines, which motivates the test of the photometric granularity in Section IV.1. Superluminous supernovae are defined by their luminosity [20], so that a distance is needed to estimate it, although their duration and bumps carry some information [52].

Tidal disruption events are blue, slowly fading nuclear transients [22, 64, 60], so that the position within the host separates them from the supernovae and a persistent nuclear source marks the AGN. The off-nuclear TDEs found recently [58, 59] follow a different pattern, and either layer may miss them. Cataclysmic variables are Galactic binaries with recurrent outbursts, and the absence of a host identifies them, provided that it is distinguished from a host below the limit of the catalogue.

The hold-out contains LBV outbursts, which can resemble Type IIn supernovae [63], calcium-rich transients, which are identified by their late-time spectra [13], LRNe and ILRTs, which overlap faint red supernovae, the rapidly evolving FBOT AT 2018cow [30], and classical novae, i.e. thermonuclear outbursts in CV systems. These physical distinctions motivate the tests of the following sections, while the separability of each family is measured empirically.

### II.3 Host-galaxy context

We use four external blocks, i.e. the Pan-STARRS host photometry and angular offset, a photometric redshift from the Legacy Surveys, the Gaia and WISE point-source context, and a Pan-STARRS pre-outburst counterpart, and we give their query definitions, match rates and catalogue limitations in Appendix D. The photometric redshift supplies a pseudo-absolute magnitude,

$$ M_{\mathrm{pseudo}}=m_{\mathrm{peak}}-5\log_{10}\!\left[d_{L}(z_{\mathrm{phot}})/10\,\mathrm{pc}\right], $$

where $d_{L}$ is the luminosity distance in a flat $\Lambda$ CDM cosmology with $H_{0}=70\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$ and $\Omega_{m}=0.3$ . Spectroscopic redshifts enter only the reference comparison of Section IV.2, because their availability depends strongly on the class (Section VII.1); at deployment, a known host redshift can replace the photometric one, a substitution that lies outside the benchmark evaluated here.

The host offset separates nuclear from displaced events, the WISE colour marks persistent AGN activity, and the pre-outburst counterpart reveals quiescent binaries and nuclei. The missing blocks are kept and handled by the context dropout of Section III.3, and since a nearest-source association can select the wrong galaxy, a change of catalogue or of association rule requires the corresponding features to be refitted.

## III Methods

### III.1 Light-curve representation

From each light curve, i.e. a set of irregularly sampled measurements $(t,\mathrm{flux},\sigma_{\mathrm{flux}},\mathrm{band})$ , we compute $160$ features, which include the per-band statistics of the light-curve library [43], fits of the Bazin function [5], colours and their evolution, and descriptors of the cadence. Missing bands and failed fits are kept as NaN values, which gradient-boosted trees [37] handle natively.

For the neural network that we use in the comparison of Section IV.4 and for the retrieval of similar objects, we also interpolate the $g$ and $r$ bands onto a grid of $64$ points over the $100$ -day window and normalise each object, so that the grid describes only the shape of the light curve. The $i$ band is too sparse for a grid (Section II) and enters only through the features.

### III.2 Hierarchical classifier

We predict in two stages, i.e. a five-way classifier over $\{$ SN Ia, SN CC+, AGN, TDE, CV $\}$ , where SN CC+ combines SN CC and SLSN, followed by a binary classifier within SN CC+, so that

$$ P(\mathrm{SLSN})=P(\mathrm{SN\,CC}^{+})\,P(\mathrm{SLSN}\mid\mathrm{SN\,CC}^{+}). $$

Both stages are LightGBM models [37] with class weights $w_{c}\propto(1/n_{c})^{\beta}$ , and the binary branch is tuned on the area under the curve, because its positive fraction is only $5.7\%$ . The hyperparameters are tuned once with Optuna [2] on a held-out validation split and are then kept fixed. Section IV.1 evaluates the taxonomy, and Section IV.4 compares the estimators.

### III.3 External-context dropout

The host photometry, the photometric redshift, the point-source block and the pre-outburst counterpart are unavailable for a fraction of the objects. In order to prevent the model from reading the absence of a block as evidence for a class, each external block is blanked independently on a random $30\%$ of the training rows. This is the photometric counterpart of the metadata dropout of astraNet [54], which keeps the spectroscopic classifier robust when the metadata of an object are missing, and Section VII.1 shows why this decision matters.

### III.4 Anomaly layer

The anomaly layer operates on top of the trained classifier and uses luna11 1 luna was developed as part of the astraNet work, and we refer the reader to [54] for more details. The code is available at https://github.com/asasli/luna., an out-of-distribution scoring package whose scorers fall into four families [71, 54, for a taxonomy of such scorers, see]: uncertainty scores from the logits (maximum softmax probability, entropy, energy and ODIN; 28, 41, 39), distance scores in the embedding space (Mahalanobis variants, $k$ -NN and the typicality of the predicted class), density scores (Gaussian mixture, isolation forest [40], local outlier factor [9] and PCA residual), and a hybrid manifold residual. We use the fourteen scorers that a tree classifier supports, since the two others of luna require a projection head and coarse-level logits. The scorers read an embedding and a set of logits, which are the $160$ features with the raw scores of the tree model, or, for the comparison of Appendix B and the retrieval of similar objects, the penultimate layer of a two-branch network over the light-curve grid and the same features.

The anomaly layer reads a narrower feature space than the classifier, i.e. the light-curve features, the host photometry and the Gaia and WISE context, without the photometric-redshift and pre-outburst-counterpart blocks, which help the classification and measurably harm the blind detection (Section IV.2); the space used is stated next to each result.

The scores are combined either blind, i.e. as the mean percentile rank across the scorers, which requires no labelled anomalies, or by a supervised combiner (logistic regression or LightGBM) when confirmed examples exist. For the blind consensus, the percentile ranks are read from one half of the validation normals and the threshold is set on the other half, so that the score of an object does not depend on the other objects of the batch. The alarm threshold at a nominal rate $\alpha$ is the $\lceil(n+1)(1-\alpha)\rceil$ -th order statistic of the $n$ held-out validation normals, a conservative choice that gives an infinite threshold when $n$ is too small, and the false-alarm rate that each threshold realises on the independent test normals is reported next to the main detection rates (Table 8); it lies between $0.6\%$ and $1.4\%$ for a nominal $1\%$ .

### III.5 Evaluation protocols

The classification results come from five-fold cross-validation, reported as the mean and the standard deviation across folds with paired per-fold differences; unless stated otherwise, the quoted $\pm$ values are spreads across folds, draws or orderings, and intervals are given explicitly where a claim needs one. The anomaly detection is evaluated at a false-alarm budget of $1\%$ , the operating point that matters when the downstream resource is spectroscopic time, and the human review as recovery against the number of inspected objects. The anomaly experiments use three protocols, which should be compared only within their stated sample: the leave-one-class-out test, which removes a trained class and is optimistic in our experiments (Section VII.2); the genuine hold-out of $53$ objects from families absent from the taxonomy, the direct but statistically limited test of novelty; and the TDE-free protocol, in which the $57$ TDEs of the pooled training and test splits are hidden targets and the $11$ TDEs of the validation split serve as confirmed examples (Table 6 in Appendix A).

### IV.3 Calibrated prediction sets

*Figure 3: Class-conditional conformal prediction on the headline classifier, out of fold. Left: empirical per-class coverage against the nominal level for two miscoverage rates. Right: mean prediction-set size per true class: an SLSN receives on average $1.7$ candidate labels at $\alpha=0.10$ , typically $\{$ SLSN, SN CC $\}$ , mirroring Fig. 2. Mean sizes below one at $\alpha=0.32$ reflect empty sets.*

Follow-up schedulers and population studies need calibrated uncertainties in addition to the most probable class. For this reason, the classifier reports class-conditional (Mondrian) conformal prediction sets [66, 3]: for each class, the nonconformity $1-p_{c}$ is calibrated separately, and the prediction set contains every class whose probability exceeds its own threshold. The class-conditional construction is important here, since a single marginal guarantee would be dominated by the SN Ia and could leave the rare classes under-covered.

At level $\alpha$ , a finite class-conditional threshold requires $n_{c}\geq\lceil 1/\alpha\rceil-1$ calibration members, i.e. nine at $\alpha=0.10$ , and a simple calibration split leaves only seven TDEs. For this reason, we use the out-of-fold scores of a five-fold cross-fit within each outer training portion; the dropout affects only the fitting rows, and the outer test objects stay outside both fitting and calibration. This construction is related to cross-conformal prediction [68, 4], and we report the empirical coverage without claiming a finite-sample guarantee. The deployed module uses the same construction over the training and validation splits together.

The result is shown in Fig. 3. At a nominal coverage of $90\%$ , the marginal empirical coverage is $90.2\%$ and $78.9\%$ of the objects receive a single label. The per-class coverages are $89.8\%$ , $91.1\%$ , $96.8\%$ , $90.0\%$ , $86.8\%$ and $89.8\%$ for SN Ia, SN CC, SLSN, AGN, TDE and CV, respectively. Thus the cross-conformal construction does not achieve the nominal level in every class; the TDE estimate is based on only $68$ objects. The classes that the confusion matrix shows to be entangled are exactly the ones that are delivered as candidate sets, which is the appropriate hand-off to spectroscopy.

Each report states the nominal level, the empirical true-class coverage of the predicted class, the credibility, i.e. the largest class $p$ -value, and the confidence, i.e. one minus the second-largest $p$ -value; the coverage measures how often the set contains the true class, which is a different quantity from the precision of the predicted label. Appendix F shows with one object why the four numbers are reported together.

### IV.4 Comparison with sequence models

We compare the trees with the released AppleCiDEr transformer [36], retrained with its own recipe on the same objects, taxonomy and five folds (Appendix C), since tabular trees are a strong baseline at this sample size [24]. The transformer reaches a macro $F_{1}$ of $0.64\pm 0.03$ , against $0.72\pm 0.03$ for flare with the light-curve features and $0.84\pm 0.02$ with the full context on these folds (the $0.83\pm 0.02$ of Table 2 comes from the folds of the main comparison). The paired advantage of the light-curve features is $+0.07\pm 0.02$ , positive in all five folds, with the largest gaps for the AGN and the TDEs, and this comparison supports the adopted features at the present training size.

Averaging the trees with a two-branch convolutional network improves the light-curve-only macro $F_{1}$ from $0.71$ to $0.76$ (McNemar $p=0.04$ ), while once the host context and $M_{\mathrm{pseudo}}$ are included the average no longer improves on the trees ( $0.79$ against $0.80$ , with $0.76$ for the network alone). This is consistent with an overlap between the information that the network extracts and that of the context, and for this reason we keep the trees alone; the balanced random forest and further tuning are reported in Appendix C [53, 11].

## V Anomaly detection

### V.1 Blind detection of out-of-taxonomy objects

Without any labelled anomaly, the blind consensus over the fourteen scorers behaves differently on the two halves of the hold-out, and we quote them separately, since an aggregate over the $53$ objects would be dominated by the largest family. The $37$ classical novae reach an area under the curve of $0.92$ , and $19\%$ of them (seven objects; $95\%$ interval from $9\%$ to $34\%$ ) are detected at a false-alarm budget of $1\%$ , which realises $1.1\%$ on the test normals. At budgets of $5\%$ and $10\%$ , which realise $6.5\%$ and $13\%$ , the same consensus detects $57\%$ and $81\%$ of the novae and three and five of the sixteen objects without a parent class, which is the regime in which the review loop of Section V.2 operates. The sixteen objects from the families without a parent class reach $0.73$ , with a single detection, which is too few to quote a rate, and the four families with more than one member lie close to each other, between $0.64$ and $0.75$ (the single FBOT has no area under the curve). The other rates quoted for the novae in this paper come from different protocols, which are listed in Table 6.

This difference agrees with the expectation of Section II.2, since the novel families are defined by spectroscopic observables, while the novae have a parent class in the taxonomy (Appendix A). We tested, on identical pools and thresholds, the fourteen scorers alone and in groups, five representations with and without host context, several fusion, routing and cascade rules, and synthetic outlier exposure [29], and the best configurations converge to the same values (Appendix B). Three findings explain this result. In the light-curve feature space only the uncertainty scores have probability mass in the extreme tail, so that at a $1\%$ budget the energy score, i.e. the log-sum-exp of the logits, is the only scorer with a usable detection rate. The quantities computed after the softmax lose the total-evidence scale that separates an object matching nothing from an object ambiguous between two classes. The feature-space outlier detectors used for ZTF [43] detect one or two objects at this budget. Combining the scorers creates no signal that no single scorer carries, since averaging dilutes the extreme tail, and the CVs, recovered by the density scorers and not by energy, are the one case of complementarity. The representation dominates the blind regime: the host photometry raises the blind detection of the novae from $3\%$ to $19\%$ , mainly through the absence of a host. This is what the novae share with the $304$ trained CVs, so that the blind rule detects an object without a host whose light curve does not match the CVs. The limit is unchanged when the anomaly sample is doubled with the $57$ unseen TDEs, when the scorer is chosen with an oracle, and when the $114$ peculiar sub-types are removed from the training set (Appendix B). The physical interpretation, i.e. that these families are defined by observables that two-band photometry does not carry, is plausible, but sixteen objects spread over five families are not enough to prove that they cannot be separated.

### V.2 Recovery versus review budget

We simulate the active review following Ishida et al. [32] and Lochner and Bassett [42], as an operator would carry it out in a vetting platform [62, 12, 55]. The full six-class model with host context ranks the $53$ out-of-taxonomy objects mixed with the $1575$ known-class test objects, and, starting blind, each round inspects the top $20$ remaining candidates, obtains their true labels, refits a logistic combiner on all the inspections and re-ranks the rest. The simulated operator has perfect labels, while a real confirmation may require a spectrum, so that a saving in inspections differs from a saving in telescope time.

In the TDE-free setup of Section VI, a combiner fitted on eleven confirmed TDEs, i.e. more labels but all from one class, reduces the detection of the real unknowns from $19\%$ to $7\%$ , which is consistent with learning the signature of the TDEs, whereas a handful of confirmations from several families improves four of the five held-out families.

### V.3 Retrieval of similar objects

A confirmed rarity could in principle multiply itself, if the archive were queried for the objects that resemble it and the neighbours were vetted. Retrieval works for the one family with tens of members (for the novae, seven of the twenty nearest neighbours belong to the same family) and returns almost nothing for the families of one to six members. The per-family results are given in Appendix B.

In this section, we measure what the first confirmations of a new family are worth, depending on where they are used: in a combiner over the anomaly scores, in a head on the frozen features, or as a new class of the classifier (Fig. 5; the numbers, with the realised false-alarm rates, are in Table 8 of Appendix E). We then vary the number of confirmations for the last of these options (Fig. 6).

For the TDEs (upper block of Table 8 and left panel of Fig. 5), the combiner over the anomaly scores, which is the standard few-shot approach in the out-of-distribution literature, does not improve on the blind energy rule with eleven labels. However, when the same eleven objects are added to the classifier as a new class, we detect $85\%$ of the hidden TDEs, and five of them already detect $79\%$ . With identical labels, targets and budget, the promotion improves on a logistic combiner by $29$ points ( $95\%$ interval from $17$ to $42$ ). A logistic head on the frozen features does better than the combiner, but it still remains well below the promotion.

The TDE-free setup is a deleted-class construction, which flatters the detectors (Section VII.2), and for this reason we repeat the comparison on the classical novae, which were never part of the taxonomy (lower block of Table 8). The combiner improves the detection of the novae from $12\%$ to $35\%$ , but it remains far below the $82$ – $83\%$ of the other two options. A head on the frozen features already matches the promotion, because the properties that define the novae (no host, Galactic position) are directly readable in the feature space. For the TDEs, retraining improves on the logistic head that we tested. For these two families and the models tested, using the confirmations in feature space outperforms combining anomaly scores. Retraining the classifier adds a further gain for the TDEs, while for the novae a head on the frozen features is enough.

The number of confirmations that the promotion needs can also be measured, by thinning each class in the training folds while the test fold keeps all its members (Fig. 6). If we define $N_{80}$ as the number of confirmations at which a family reaches $80\%$ detection, the TDEs need about six and the novae about sixteen, and this ordering holds at every false-alarm budget between $0.5\%$ and $5\%$ . These thinning curves use subsamples of the training folds and held-out test folds, while Table 8 uses fixed pools of draws. Therefore, the nova $N_{80}$ and the $83\%$ recovery with eleven labels in that table come from different protocols.

The difference is visible at the left edge of the curves. With no labelled member, the classifier is still trained with one output for the new class, whose probability rises only where every known class scores low (Appendix B). This zero-label score already recovers $60\%$ of the TDEs against $11\%$ of the novae. Thus, the TDEs are already isolated by the representation and need only a few labels. On the other hand, the novae are spread across several trained classes (Appendix A) and keep improving well beyond ten. The remaining families are too small for this test, and leave-one-out promotion over the members of the LBVs, LRNe, ILRTs and Ca-rich transients available in the splits ( $6$ , $4$ , $3$ and $3$ objects; Table 6 lists which Ca-rich transients enter each experiment) gives one detection in sixteen trials. Blind scoring and a trained class are therefore successive stages of one lifecycle, with the review loop of Section V.2 moving a family from the first to the second, and the slowest step is the first one, where the first members have to be found one at a time (Section V.3).

## VII Reliability failure modes

In this section, we discuss two evaluation hazards that we encountered, i.e. the class-dependent availability of the context and the use of deleted trained classes as proxies for unknown populations. Each of them would have inflated the reported performance.

### VII.1 Class-dependent missingness

Externally sourced features are often unavailable in a class-dependent way. In our catalogue, the spectroscopic redshift is present for every supernova and TDE and for none of the AGN and CVs. This is because of the way the follow-up was allocated and not because of the physics. Supplying this redshift naively to the six-class model raises the macro $F_{1}$ from $0.74$ to $0.86$ , and the AGN $F_{1}$ from $0.70$ to $0.95$ , but essentially all of this gain comes from the model reading a missing value as a class label. Restricted to the four classes where the redshift is always available, the same feature gives a real but much smaller improvement.

The host photometry carries the same hazard in a milder form, since its missingness is physical (a CV has no host galaxy), but the depth of the survey still makes the absence of a detected host unreliable. Without the dropout of Section III.3, the host features improve the objects that have a host and degrade those that do not, with a macro $F_{1}$ that decreases from $0.78$ to $0.73$ on the latter; with the dropout, they improve both. Reporting the performance separately for the objects with and without each external block is the diagnostic that reveals this effect.

### VII.2 Leave-one-class-out tests

Deleting a trained class and detecting its members is the standard out-of-distribution benchmark. Choosing a scorer on five deleted classes and applying it to the sixth raises the mean area under the curve from $0.75$ to $0.81$ , while the same selection on the out-of-taxonomy families lowers it from $0.62$ to $0.55$ , because in this benchmark the deleted classes are coherent and well sampled and the unknown families are small. For this reason, we report both protocols, since the deleted-class performance alone would overstate the discovery performance here.

## IX Deployment and independent validation

### IX.1 Fritz operation

The photometric module of AppleCiDEr [36] is designed to run inside the boom broker [34], and it already runs in production on Fritz [62, 12], the SkyPortal instance of the ZTF collaboration, as an analysis service that the platform dispatches to the Open Science Grid for every source saved by the participating programs. For every source, it returns the class probabilities, the prediction set with its four numbers, the anomaly $p$ -value of the blind consensus of Section V with its alarms, and a triage verdict (Fig. 8). Unlike the single reference used for Table 4, the $p$ -values are computed separately for groups of objects with a similar number of detections, since with a single reference the day- $5$ alarm fired on $10\%$ of the known objects with nine or more detections and on none of those with three or fewer. A classification is posted only when the $90\%$ set contains a single class, or the coarse label supernova when every member of the set is a supernova type. The pipeline takes about $2$ ms per object on one CPU core in batches and about $35$ ms per alert on its own, most of it in the fourteen anomaly scorers, against a mean Rubin alert rate of order $300$ s-1. The full model is retrained in minutes, so that the promotion of a new class can follow a nightly cadence.

When the first three ZTF detections of ZTF26abzxgsr, the optical counterpart of a gamma-ray burst, which were taken within an hour and a half, are replayed through the current version of the module, the consensus flags the object at a $5\%$ per-analysis false-alarm rate ( $p=0.015$ ), and its lifetime statistic reaches the monthly threshold of Section IX.3, at which $12$ of the $1\,882$ known objects are as significant, i.e. one false alarm per $21$ days on the stream, against one per $14$ days with the benchmark calibration. Its prediction set, {SN CC, CV}, contains two classes, so that no classification is posted. This is a retrospective replay on the photometry that Fritz holds, and since this object also entered the choice of Section IX.2 to keep the boosters, it illustrates the alarm and does not confirm it independently.

### IX.2 Transfer to the photometry of the service

The ZTF photometry supplied by Fritz is denser than the public-alert light curves used to build the benchmark through boom. For the benchmark test objects, it contains a median of $93$ detections within $100$ days, compared with $26$ in the benchmark; only $39\%$ of its $g$ - and $r$ -band epochs are shared with the benchmark, and $i$ -band detections are available for $45\%$ of the objects. This difference in the input affects both classification and anomaly calibration. On the same $1\,555$ BTS test objects, routed as in the service, the macro $F_{1}$ falls from $0.836$ to $0.807$ , while the realised false-alarm rate at the nominal $1\%$ rises from $0.6\%$ to $2.4\%$ .

We evaluated two responses to this shift: retraining the models on the Fritz photometry, and retaining their weights while recalibrating the anomaly layer. Full retraining restored the false-alarm rates without a clear improvement in classification across seeds, but no longer flagged the gamma-ray burst discussed in Section IX. We therefore retained the classifiers and anomaly boosters and recalibrated the anomaly layer on the photometry supplied by Fritz. For each of the four phase models, the consensus ranks and detection-count-dependent $p$ -values use separate halves of the validation split. The test objects enter neither stage. On the $1\,882$ BTS and Fritz test objects, the recalibrated alarm realises false-alarm rates of $0.6\%$ , $3.3\%$ and $8.2\%$ at nominal levels of $1\%$ , $5\%$ and $10\%$ , respectively, with unchanged classifications.

This recalibration concerns the anomaly alarm, not the classification prediction sets. The full-curve classifier’s nominal $90\%$ sets contain the true class for only $83\%$ of the Fritz test objects. The benchmark coverage reported in Section IV.3 therefore does not transfer directly to the service population. The prediction sets require their own calibration on representative Fritz sources.

### IX.3 False-alarm rate per unit time

Repeated analyses increase the number of false alarms that reach the reviewer. In our replay of the Fritz photometry, a nominal $1\%$ per-analysis alarm flags about $10\%$ of the known-class sources at least once within $100$ days. At the observed arrival rate of $6.8$ saved sources per day, this corresponds to roughly five false alarms per week. A threshold for a single analysis therefore does not describe the workload of a service that revisits each source as its light curve grows.

To express that workload directly, we calibrate the alarm over the full sequence of analyses and report its false-alarm rate per unit time, following the background-rate interpretation used in gravitational-wave searches [1]. The lifetime statistic $P_{\mathrm{life}}$ summarises the most significant departure from the known population over the observed history of a source. Its calibration uses replayed known-class light curves: the fraction whose whole-life statistic is at least as extreme, multiplied by the source arrival rate, gives the estimated false-alarm rate. This is an empirical calibration for the replay’s observing schedule and $100$ -day horizon, not an anytime-valid $p$ -value [35]. Appendix E gives the construction and evaluation protocol.

We evaluated thresholds targeting one false alarm per week, per month and per quarter using two-fold cross-fitting. Each known-class object was evaluated with a reference and thresholds constructed from the opposite half of the sample. The three thresholds flagged $39$ , $14$ and $11$ of the $1\,882$ objects, respectively. At the measured arrival rate, these counts correspond to approximately one false alarm every $7$ , $20$ and $25$ days. The weekly threshold therefore matches its intended rate in this replay. The monthly estimate is consistent with its target within the sampling uncertainty, but the quarterly threshold does not achieve its target (Appendix E). These time intervals also depend on the source arrival rate and must be updated if the stream changes.

The service uses the weekly threshold to send sources for expert review. With the shipped reference, this threshold recovers $27$ of the $78$ out-of-taxonomy objects ( $35\%$ , with a $95\%$ interval of $25$ – $46\%$ ), predominantly novae and two fast blue optical transients. The nominal monthly and quarterly thresholds recover $13$ and $4$ objects. The spectroscopically defined families remain undetected, consistent with the benchmark results (Fig. 9).

### IX.4 Transfer of the learning from confirmations

The two supervised steps of Sections V.2 and VI transfer to this stream as well. The review loop, run on the same $1\,960$ objects with the Fritz photometry and the same protocol, recovers $42\%$ of the $78$ out-of-taxonomy objects after $100$ inspections and $71\%$ after $250$ , against $37\%$ and $55\%$ for the static ranking by the consensus. Therefore, the gain of the loop appears later than on the benchmark and reaches the same size. A logistic combiner over the fourteen scores, fitted on the known objects of the validation split and on the $50$ out-of-taxonomy objects of the benchmark and applied to the $28$ Fritz objects that it never saw, detects $17$ of them at a realised $5\%$ against $11$ for the blind consensus, with the same three detections outside the novae. This transfer of the first confirmations between populations is what the deployed module uses to order its review queue.

## X Discussion

In the alert stream, the photometric ranking complements the image-based filters that select the real and bright transients [16, 51]. In our benchmark, about one in three of the first hundred candidates of the consensus ranking lies outside the taxonomy, against one in thirty-one in the whole evaluation stream. Active review further raises this yield, and spectroscopy confirms the candidates. A promoted class also needs at least nine calibration members before its class-conditional threshold at $\alpha=0.10$ becomes finite, which is distinct from the number of labels that its detection needs.

The comparison of the uses of the labels is the central practical result of this work. Both families benefit more from learning in the feature space than from combining the anomaly scores, and only the TDEs show a clear additional gain from retraining over the frozen-feature head that we tested. The recovery-versus-budget curves and $N_{80}$ are useful measures for repeating this comparison in other surveys, while their numerical values describe the present samples and protocols.

The main limitations come from the size and the selection of the samples. The rarest families contain one to six objects, too few to establish a general photometric detection limit, and the review loop assumes perfect labels at a prevalence of $3.3\%$ , much higher than in a raw alert stream, where the first rounds would return fewer confirmations. The early-time study selects the objects by their eventual light-curve quality, and the transfer to the photometry of the service shows that both the false-alarm rates and the prediction-set coverage change with the input (Sections IX.2 and IX.3). A larger hold-out, for example from the Transient Name Server [21], would require a matched reference population, and the six-band light curves of the Rubin Observatory [33], as well as sequence models pre-trained on much larger unlabelled samples, may change the comparisons of this work.

Finally, the first population on which the method can produce new results is the $7\,631$ BTS objects that never received a spectrum, which are half a magnitude fainter than the benchmark and were selected by the same survey under the same criteria. The objects whose prediction set excludes their own most probable class and the top of the anomaly ranking form a target list for spectroscopy, once the false-alarm threshold has been recalibrated on classified objects of matched magnitude, and we leave these results to a companion paper.

## XI Conclusions

We have introduced flare, which combines photometric classification, anomaly ranking and learning from confirmed candidates, and we have followed transient novelty from blind detection through human review to supervised classification on one stream of ZTF data. Catalogue context raises the classification where the defining property of a class is absent from the light curve; blind detection recovers few objects of the smallest unknown families, while a simulated review loop recovers most of the hold-out for a small fraction of the inspections; and the first confirmations of a new family are most useful in the feature space, with an additional gain from retraining that depends on the family.

These results suggest a practical sequence: rank the unlabelled candidates for review, and learn from their features as the confirmations accumulate. The deployment on Fritz shows that the module operates in production, and the transfer to the photometry of the service shows that the calibration has to be made on that photometry and that an alarm of a service which re-analyses its sources is best reported as a false-alarm rate per unit time. We expect that this framework will be very useful for the Rubin era, where the path of an unknown object from the first alarm to a trained class has to be short.

The zero-label score of Section VI follows from the training of the trees. With one output for the new class and no member of it, the probability of that class is

$$ P_{\rm new}=\frac{e^{z_{\rm new}}}{\sum_{k}e^{z_{k}}}, $$

where $z_{k}$ are the raw scores of the trees. The raw score $z_{\rm new}$ starts from the boosting initialisation and is penalised on the known-class training objects since its gradient under the cross-entropy loss is $P_{\rm new}$ itself for every training object. Therefore, it stays low wherever the training data lie and $P_{\rm new}$ rises only where all the known classes also score low.

For the retrieval of Section V.3, measured with cosine nearest neighbours in the embedding of the network over the same stream, the precision at ten neighbours for same-family retrieval is $0.31$ against a chance rate of $0.016$ , but Table 7 shows that this comes from one family. A confirmed nova returns seven more novae among its twenty nearest neighbours, while a confirmed LBV returns none, so that the families that most need to grow are those too sparse for their members to be each other’s neighbours.

## Appendix C Model comparisons

This appendix contains the comparisons behind Section IV.4.

The AppleCiDEr photometric classifier was retrained with the configuration of its release [36]. Each detection becomes a token built from the time since the first detection and since the previous detection (both as $\log(1+\Delta t)$ ), the log-flux and its uncertainty, and a one-hot band. The times also enter through a Time2Vec embedding, and the encoder has four layers of dimension $128$ with eight heads, a class token and a dropout of $0.3$ . On each fold, the encoder is first pre-trained for $50$ epochs to reconstruct $30\%$ of masked detections, and is then fine-tuned with a focal loss ( $\gamma=2$ ), a class-balanced sampler and early stopping on the same early-stopping objects that the trees use. The only changes from the release are the six classes of this work in place of five and the $100$ -day window. The per-class $F_{1}$ is $0.93$ for the SN Ia, $0.74$ for the SN CC, $0.36$ for the SLSNe, $0.59$ for the AGN, $0.45$ for the TDEs and $0.81$ for the CVs.

Copying a number from the published alerce light-curve classifier [53, 17] would confound the taxonomy, the sample selection and the photometry with the estimator, and for this reason we replace only the estimator, i.e. we train the balanced random forest [11, 8] that alerce uses, in a flat and in a balanced-hierarchical arrangement, on the identical folds, features, context blocks and dropout. Both forests reach a macro $F_{1}$ of $0.74\pm 0.02$ , against $0.83\pm 0.02$ for the boosted trees, and the difference is concentrated on the rare classes (a TDE $F_{1}$ of about $0.65$ against $0.81$ , and an SLSN $F_{1}$ of about $0.32$ against $0.53$ ). With the same hyperparameter search that our trees received, the hierarchical forest improves to $0.76\pm 0.02$ , which still leaves a deficit that is positive in every fold.

Finally, the trees themselves leave little room for improvement: a five-seed ensemble and a new hyperparameter search change the macro $F_{1}$ by at most $0.002$ , adding nine Gaussian-process summaries of the kind used in the PLAsTiCC challenge [7, 38, 31] lowers it slightly, and the fusion with a dilated-convolution (TCN) branch becomes slightly positive only once the point-source block is included ( $+0.008\pm 0.011$ ), well within the fold-to-fold spread.

## Appendix D Catalogue construction

For the host photometry, we query Pan-STARRS DR2 [10] within $30^{\prime\prime}$ of every position and record the nearest extended source ( $i_{\mathrm{PSF}}-i_{\mathrm{Kron}}>0.05$ ), i.e. its angular offset, its Kron magnitudes and colours, and the number of extended neighbours. Of the $10\,497$ positions, $10\,487$ return a field and $10\,229$ contain an extended source. The resulting statistics follow the physics of the classes: TDEs and AGN lie on their host (median offsets of $0.12^{\prime\prime}$ and $0.14^{\prime\prime}$ ), supernovae are displaced by $3$ – $4^{\prime\prime}$ , the hosts of SLSNe are two magnitudes fainter than the average host, and only $77\%$ of the CVs have any extended source nearby, at a median separation of $15^{\prime\prime}$ . This nearest-source rule will assign the wrong host to some offset transients near bright galaxies; probabilistic associations, such as the host matching that the Transient Name Server now publishes [72], are better, but they cannot be substituted into these columns, since the Legacy Surveys model magnitudes are $0.25$ mag brighter than the Pan-STARRS Kron magnitudes of the same galaxy (scatter $0.19$ mag) and the two catalogues select a different nearest galaxy for a quarter of the sample, so that adopting them requires refitting the host block.

Photometric redshifts come from Legacy Surveys DR10, with DR9 as the northern fallback [15, 73]. We select the nearest extended source carrying a photo- $z$ : $8891$ positions return a field and $7582$ yield a usable value. Equation (1) converts the observed peak to $M_{\mathrm{pseudo}}$ . The median photo- $z$ is $0.32$ for SLSNe and $0.05$ for core-collapse supernovae, consistent with the larger accessible volume for luminous events.

For the point-source context, Gaia DR3 [19] within $2^{\prime\prime}$ provides the parallax and the proper motion with their significances, the $G$ magnitude, the RUWE, and, more informatively than any of these quantities, the presence of a point source at all: $98\%$ of the AGN and $84\%$ of the TDEs have a Gaia counterpart (a nuclear point source), against $8$ – $21\%$ of the supernovae and $18\%$ of the CVs, whose quiescent counterparts mostly lie below the Gaia limit. AllWISE [69] within $6^{\prime\prime}$ provides the mid-infrared colour $W1-W2$ , which is the classical AGN discriminant [61]: $42\%$ of the AGN have $W1-W2>0.8$ against at most $2\%$ of every other class.

For the pre-outburst counterpart, Pan-STARRS reaches about $2.5$ magnitudes deeper than the point-source limit of Gaia and its $3\pi$ survey of 2010–2014 [10] precedes every transient in the sample, so that a source within $1.5^{\prime\prime}$ of the position is a candidate counterpart (the quiescent binary of a CV, a massive progenitor or a persistent nucleus); the same DR2 query provides it, and $41\%$ of the positions carry one. All four blocks are externally sourced and unevenly available, which makes them the natural setting for the missingness failure mode of Section VII.1.

## Appendix E Replay protocol and the use of the first labels

The replay of Section IX.3 analyses every light curve at every detection up to the fortieth and at every fifth detection afterwards; each prefix is routed to the phase model that its span selects, and its per-analysis $p$ -value $p_{k}$ comes from the consensus of that model, calibrated on the validation split (Section IX.2). At the $k$ -th analysis, the running minimum is $m_{k}=\min_{j\leq k}p_{j}$ , and its lifetime $p$ -value is

$$ \pi_{k}=\frac{1+\#\{i:m^{\mathrm{ref}}_{i,k}\leq m_{k}\}}{1+N_{k}}, $$

where $m^{\mathrm{ref}}_{i,k}$ are the running minima of the $N_{k}$ known reference objects that reach the $k$ -th analysis (beyond the analysis index that at least $50$ of them reach, the last such index is used); the lifetime statistic is $P_{\mathrm{life}}=\min_{k}\pi_{k}$ over the analyses so far. The false-alarm rate reported for an object is $(1+\#\{i:P^{\mathrm{ref}}_{\mathrm{life},i}\leq P_{\mathrm{life}}\})/(1+N)$ , computed over the whole-life statistics of the $N$ known reference objects, times the rate at which sources enter the service, and the threshold of each level is the corresponding quantile of $P^{\mathrm{ref}}_{\mathrm{life}}$ . The schedule depends only on the number of detections, so that a new detection adds analyses without removing any and an alarm reached at an earlier analysis is kept; beyond the fortieth detection, the newest detections enter $P_{\mathrm{life}}$ at the next multiple of five. At analysis time the deployed module replays the prefixes of the light curve with the same schedule, which takes about two seconds, so that the service keeps no state between analyses. The reference that the module ships uses all $1\,882$ known test objects, so we verified the levels of Section IX.3 by cross-fitting on two halves: the running-minimum reference and the thresholds are built from one half of the test objects, each object of the other half is evaluated once, under a reference that excludes it, and the two held-out halves together give one evaluation of every test object. Since the per-analysis $p$ -values come from the validation split alone, no stage of the calibration sees the evaluated object. The pooled held-out counts of Section IX.3, $39$ , $14$ and $11$ of $1\,882$ , have approximate Wilson intervals of $1.5$ – $2.8\%$ , $0.4$ – $1.2\%$ and $0.3$ – $1.0\%$ , approximate because the two folds share the objects in their reference and evaluation roles, so that the quarterly interval excludes its target of $0.2\%$ .

## Appendix F Reading a single report

A classical nova hidden in the test stream shows why the four numbers of Section IV.3 are reported together: its most probable class is SN Ia, but with a $p$ -value below $\alpha$ , so that the prediction set excludes the class that the classifier reports, and its credibility, $0.14$ , is about a quarter of the median credibility of the SN Ia in the test split ( $0.50$ ). Empty sets at looser levels mark objects that match nothing well, although the set size alone is a weak anomaly score (Section V.1). The probabilities of the trees are already well calibrated (top-label expected calibration error $0.0093$ ). As novelty scores, the width of the Venn–Abers interval of the predicted class [67] and the sets of a split class-conditional density-ratio construction [25], calibrated on an independent half of the validation objects, reach areas under the curve of $0.82$ and $0.59$ on the $53$ out-of-taxonomy objects and detect none of the sixteen objects without a parent class at a nominal $1\%$ false-alarm threshold.

# Machine learning reconstruction of cosmic ray parameters in EAS at HAWC

**Authors:** I. Torres

## Abstract

The High-Altitude Water Cherenkov (HAWC) Observatory comprises 300 water Cherenkov detectors, each equipped with four photomultipliers, located on the Volcán Sierra Negra in Mexico at 4,100 masl. This observatory can detect gamma rays in an energy range from 300 GeV to 100 TeV and cosmic rays from 100 GeV to 1 PeV. One of HAWC’s primary challenges is characterizing air showers and estimate their physical parameters, a highly complex task due to the nature of the data and the processes involved. Currently, HAWC employs two energy estimators for gamma rays: the ground parameter method and a neural network-based approach. However, for cosmic rays, only the likelihood-based estimator is available. In this work, we leverage machine learning techniques to achieve more accurate estimation of the physical parameters of cosmic rays. These techniques are explored as an alternative for reconstructing the physical properties of extensive air showers using simulated data aligned with the observatory’s configuration. Various models were trained and evaluated through an optimized pipeline and the most effective one was selected as the final implementation after a comprehensive comparison. This approach improves the accuracy of physical parameter estimation, contributing significantly to the detailed characterization of cosmic ray events.

## 1 Introduction

### 

Cosmic rays (CRs) with energies between $\sim 10^{11.5}$ and $10^{16.5}~\mathrm{eV}$ per nucleon span the region of the all-particle spectrum where the so-called knee appears, and where the transition from Galactic to potentially extragalactic accelerators is expected. Accurate measurements of the total flux and elemental composition within this energy range are therefore pivotal for discriminating among competing models of CR acceleration and propagation. Ground-based observatories, such as the High-Altitude Water Cherenkov (HAWC) Observatory, record the footprints of extensive air showers (EAS) produced when primary particles interact with the atmosphere. The collected information, time and charge measurements, can be translated into estimations of the main EAS parameters, the most relevant of which are the primary energy, the arrival direction, and core position.

### 

HAWC is designed to detect high-energy gamma rays and cosmic rays. It is located on the slope of the Sierra Negra volcano in Puebla, Mexico, at an elevation of 4100 m a.s.l. HAWC’s elevation allows for efficient detection of the secondary particles produced before they are significantly absorbed by the atmosphere. The array comprises 300 water Cherenkov detectors (WCDs), each 7.3 m in diameter and 4.5 m in height, covering an area of 22,000 $m^{2}$ . Each tank is instrumented with four upward-facing photomultiplier tubes (PMTs), which capture the Cherenkov light produced by the secondary particles of the EAS traveling through the water [1]. HAWC is sensitive to showers induced by cosmic rays ranging from TeV to a few PeV energies [2]. The extensive data set collected by the observatory allows us to develop advanced reconstruction methods, including machine learning algorithms, to improve the measurements of the shower parameters, such as the energy estimator for gamma rays [3] and cosmic rays [4].

### 

The first cosmic-ray energy estimator implemented in HAWC is a traditional model that chooses the maximum likelihood match between the detected shower and four-dimensional probability tables11 1 The dimensions mentioned are the zenith angle, primary energy, distance from the HAWC central array to the shower core position, and PMT signal amplitude. [2]. The first attempt to provide an alternative cosmic-ray energy estimator using machine learning techniques was reported at the previous ICRC [4], with the objective of obtaining a more accurate prediction of this observable. In this contribution, we present an update on the application of a Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) for predicting cosmic-ray energy. We report three models trained with TensorFlow, which allows the development of more complex architectures and other characteristics (more details are provided in Section 3). These models were trained and evaluated using HAWC simulation data. To ensure a robust assessment, the models were also applied to one day of HAWC data to obtain the cosmic-ray spectrum. The comparative analysis between the machine learning models and the official cosmic-ray energy estimator is provided in Section 4. Finally, in Section 5, we summarize this contribution.

## 2 Data Set

### 

Two types of data were used in this contribution: simulation and real data, both of which were produced following the HAWC official procedure [5]. Eight cosmic-ray particles (hydrogen, helium, carbon, oxygen, neon, magnesium, silicon, and iron) were simulated with energies between $\sim$ 5 GeV and 2 PeV, following a power-law spectrum with an index of -2. The hadronic model specified in CORSIKA is FLUKA and QGSJET-II-04 for low and high energies, respectively, with zenith angles ranging from $0^{\circ}$ to $60^{\circ}$ [6]. The number of remaining events after the reconstruction process is 14 million22 2 Half of the total events are protons.. On the other hand, one complete day of HAWC data was used to perform a robust evaluation of the MLP models.

## 3 Multilayer Perceptron (MLP)

### 

The machine learning model used in this contribution is the MLP. Three models were implemented using the same architecture and training specifications; the difference lies in how the input information is provided. For these models, there is a common set of input features: the total charge collected by the detectors within nine concentric annuli around the shower core [5]; the amplitude of the core fit to a simplified Nishimura–Kamata–Greisen (NKG) function [3]; and the perceptual area activated during the event. The differing input information includes the fraction of PMTs activated ( $f_{hit}$ ), the arrival direction, and the core position. In these cases, feature transformations are applied to vary the input representations across the models (see Table 1). The input parameters of each model were normalized using the $z$ -score method, which rescales each feature to have zero mean and unit variance [7].

The feature transformations used are: the fraction of PMTs activated ( $f_{hit}$ ), the cosine of the zenith angle, and the distance between the core position and the center of the HAWC array ( $R_{core}$ ).*

### 

The architecture implemented is $x:256:128:64:32:1$ , where $x$ is the number of input parameters; there are four hidden dense layers with ReLU activation functions and one linear output layer that provides an estimation of the energy based on the input information. During the training stage, Mean Squared Error (MSE) was used as the loss function, Stochastic Gradient Descent as the optimization algorithm, a learning rate of 0.01, and a maximum of 15 epochs with batches of 64. The data was split into three groups: 64%, 16%, and 20% for training, validation, and evaluation, respectively. Events from eight species were used, selecting those that passed successful reconstruction of the core and arrival direction, with a minimum fraction of 20% of PMTs with signal relative to the total array ( $f_{hit}>0.2$ ), zenith angles from $0^{\circ}$ to $35^{\circ}$ , and at least 40 PMTs with signal within a radius of 40 meters from the shower core [6].

## 4 Analysis and Results

### 

As mentioned in the previous section, the MLPs were trained using simulations of eight species to provide a comprehensive overview of the behavior of these particles. However, in the evaluation phase, only proton events are reported. Figure 1 shows the correlation between reconstructed energy and true energy for the Likelihood method and the three MLP models. In HAWC, the official cosmic-ray energy estimator is the Likelihood method. However, due to a recent software update aimed at improving gamma-ray source analysis, the performance of the Likelihood estimator has decreased. This can be seen in Figure 1(a), where there is a region in which the event prediction is almost one order of magnitude lower than the true value. On the other hand, the MLPs address this inconsistency by reducing this region and pushing those events closer to the identity line (Figures 1(b), 1(c), and 1(d) correspond to the MLP-V1, MLP-V2, and MLP-V3 models, respectively). These observations are supported by Figure 2, where the mean bias ( $\langle\Delta\log_{10}(\text{E/GeV})\rangle$ , top panel) and energy resolution ( $\sigma[\Delta\log_{10}(\text{E/GeV})]$ , bottom panel) are computed in energy bins. The MLP models show a lower mean bias value than the Likelihood estimator, meaning they provide estimates closer to the true value at lower energies. Furthermore, the models group the events closer to the ideal reconstruction line, as reflected in the bottom panel, where the energy resolution is improved across all energy bins.

### 

The robust evaluation consists of testing the models with real data. For faster comparison between models, one day of HAWC real data is used to reconstruct the cosmic-ray spectrum. The spectrum is obtained using the Unfolding method, following the procedure described in [6, 2]. In this contribution, we report the output model distributions (Figure 3(a)) and the unfolded spectrum (Figure 3(b)). The distributions show consistency across all models, with small fluctuations in some energy ranges. On the other hand, the spectra from the MLP models are in good agreement with the official energy reconstructor, Likelihood method. These models show small fluctuations similar to those observed in the histogram distributions.

In summary, all models report the same behavior, indicating that the new MLP models are consistent with the Likelihood method. This consistency suggests that the trained models are robust and reliable.*

## 5 Discussion and conclusion

### 

Supervised machine learning algorithms have improved in recent years. They have demonstrated the ability to predict values based on input information and, in many cases, provide better results than classical techniques. In this contribution, the MLP model, using TensorFlow package for training, was explored to address a regression task at the HAWC observatory; this task is to estimate the energy of the detected cosmic-ray events. Three MLPs were trained using simulations of eight particle types, with the same training configuration but varying the input feature transformations. These models were compared to the official cosmic-ray energy estimator, Likelihood, using both simulated and real HAWC data. According to the simulation results, the three MLPs achieved a lower mean bias at lower energies, indicating better accuracy in event energy estimation and improved energy resolution, which suggests greater confidence in the predictions (see Figures 1 and 2).

### 

A robust evaluation was performed by computing the cosmic-ray spectrum using one day of HAWC real data. This process makes it possible to determine whether the models were properly trained, whether the MLPs simply memorized the events or began to overfit or underfit the data. Figure 3 shows the output distributions of the Likelihood and the three MLP models, along with their corresponding spectra computed using the unfolding technique. From both figures, it can be concluded that the MLP models produce consistent results, as they follow the same behavior as the Likelihood method. These results suggest that the MLP models provide a reliable alternative for estimating the energy of cosmic-ray-induced showers. Moreover, the improved performance of the MLPs (reflected in lower estimation errors, better mean bias, and higher confidence in the energy predictions, better energy resolution) makes them a promising option for future updates of the energy reconstruction method.
